options: It is one appellation covering seven climats
Each climat is a separate appellation
It lies on the left bank of the Serein
questions.explain: Chablis Grand Cru is a single appellation with seven climats on the right bank, all Chardonnay.

cards.b: Chardonnay. All four levels, from Petit Chablis to Chablis Grand Cru, are Chardonnay only.

cards.f: On which river does Chablis lie?
cards.b: The Serein, in the Yonne department.
Upper Jurassic marl and limestone full of the fossil oyster Exogyra virgula. It underlies Chablis, Premier Cru and Grand Cru.

cards.f: Where else does the Kimmeridgian layer appear?
cards.b: In the Aube vineyards of Champagne and in Sancerre.
Younger, harder Jurassic limestone on the Chablis plateaux, where most Petit Chablis grows.

cards.f: What are the four levels of Chablis, from lowest to highest?
cards.b: Petit Chablis, Chablis, Chablis Premier Cru and Chablis Grand Cru.

cards.f: What is the main vineyard hazard in Chablis?
cards.b: Spring frost. Growers use heaters among the vines or sprinklers that coat the buds in protective ice.

cards.f: What is the typical style of Chablis?
cards.b: Pale, with high acidity and green apple and citrus fruit, often called flinty or saline. Most is made without new oak.

cards.f: How many grand cru climats does Chablis have?
cards.b: Seven, all inside the single Chablis Grand Cru appellation.

cards.f: Name the seven Chablis grand cru climats.
cards.b: Blanchot, Bougros, Les Clos, Grenouilles, Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir.

cards.f: Where is the Chablis grand cru slope?
cards.b: A single hillside on the right bank of the Serein, facing south-west over the town.
The largest Chablis grand cru climat, often the most powerful and slow to open.
A monopole lying across Vaudésir and Preuses. It is not an official grand cru climat.

cards.f: Name three right bank Chablis premiers crus.
cards.b: Fourchaume, Mont de Milieu and Montée de Tonnerre.

cards.f: Name three left bank Chablis premiers crus.
cards.b: Vaillons, Montmains and Côte de Léchet.

cards.f: How many Chablis premier cru climats are there?
cards.b: 40 climats. Many smaller ones may be sold under the name of one of 17 main premiers crus.
Village appellation in the Yonne for red wine from Pinot Noir, with up to 10% César allowed.
Burgundy's only Sauvignon appellation: white wine from Sauvignon Blanc and Sauvignon Gris.
Appellation in the Yonne for white wine from Chardonnay.

cards.f: Which regional names add a local place in the Yonne?
cards.b: Bourgogne Côtes d'Auxerre, Chitry, Coulanges-la-Vineuse, Epineuil, Tonnerre and Côte Saint-Jacques.

lessons.title: The Côte de Nuits
lessons.intro: This lesson walks the Côte de Nuits village by village from Marsannay in the north to Nuits-Saint-Georges in the south, with the grands crus of each.

p: The Côte de Nuits runs from Marsannay, just south of Dijon, to Corgoloin. The slope is narrow and the wine is almost all red Pinot Noir. Of the 32 Côte d'Or grands crus, 24 lie here.

Marsannay is the only village appellation of the Côte d'Or for red, white and rosé. Fixin makes firm reds, with premiers crus such as Clos de la Perrière and Clos Napoléon. Côte de Nuits-Villages comes from the villages at either end: Fixin and Brochon in the north, Premeaux-Prissey, Comblanchien and Corgoloin in the south.

Gevrey-Chambertin is the largest village of the Côte de Nuits and has nine grands crus. Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Bèze are the most famous, and Clos de Bèze may also be sold as Chambertin. Most grands crus lie south of the village, towards Morey.

The others are Chapelle, Charmes, Griotte, Latricières, Mazis, Mazoyères and Ruchottes, each followed by -Chambertin. Mazoyères-Chambertin may be sold as Charmes-Chambertin. The premier cru Clos Saint-Jacques, on the slope north-west of the village, is often priced like a grand cru. Gevrey reds are powerful and structured, with dark fruit.

Morey-Saint-Denis has four grands crus of its own: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos de Tart, a monopole, and Clos des Lambrays, raised to grand cru in 1981. A small part of Bonnes-Mares also lies in Morey.

Chambolle-Musigny has two grands crus. Bonnes-Mares lies at the northern end, next to Morey. Musigny lies at the southern end, next to the Clos de Vougeot, and is also known for a rare white wine. The premier cru Les Amoureuses sits just below Musigny. Chambolle reds are known for perfume and a silky texture.

The Clos de Vougeot is a walled grand cru of about 50 ha, built by the Cistercians. It runs from the upper slope down to the main road and is split among many owners, so quality depends on position and producer. Its château is home to the Confrérie des Chevaliers du Tastevin. Vougeot village wines include a white premier cru, Le Clos Blanc.

Vosne-Romanée has six grands crus. Romanée-Conti and La Tâche are monopoles of the Domaine de la Romanée-Conti. La Romanée and La Grande Rue are also monopoles, and La Grande Rue became grand cru in 1992. Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant complete the group.

Echezeaux and Grands-Echezeaux lie in the commune of Flagey-Echezeaux, whose village wine is sold as Vosne-Romanée. Leading premiers crus include Cros Parantoux, Les Suchots, Les Beaux Monts and Aux Malconsorts.

The town of Nuits-Saint-Georges gives the Côte de Nuits its name and is a centre for négociants. The appellation has no grands crus but many premiers crus. The most famous, Les Saint-Georges, Les Vaucrains and Les Cailles, lie south of the town.

The appellation continues into Premeaux-Prissey, with premiers crus such as Clos de la Maréchale, Clos Arlot and Clos des Forêts Saint-Georges. The reds are firm, dense and earthy, and need time in bottle.

key: The Côte de Nuits runs from Marsannay to Corgoloin and holds 24 of the 32 Côte d'Or grands crus, almost all red.
Marsannay is the only Côte d'Or village appellation for red, white and rosé.
Gevrey-Chambertin has nine grands crus; Clos de Bèze may be sold as Chambertin and Mazoyères as Charmes-Chambertin.
Morey-Saint-Denis: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos de Tart, Clos des Lambrays (1981) and part of Bonnes-Mares.
Chambolle-Musigny: Musigny and Bonnes-Mares; Les Amoureuses is its most famous premier cru.
Vosne-Romanée has six grands crus; Echezeaux and Grands-Echezeaux lie in Flagey-Echezeaux. Nuits-Saint-Georges has none.

questions.q: What makes Marsannay unique among Côte d'Or village appellations?
options: It has the most grands crus
It covers red, white and rosé
It is for white wine only
questions.explain: Marsannay is the only village appellation of the Côte d'Or that includes rosé as well as red and white.

questions.q: Which Gevrey grand cru may be sold under the name Charmes-Chambertin?
questions.explain: Mazoyères-Chambertin may be labelled as Charmes-Chambertin, its neighbour.

questions.q: Which Morey-Saint-Denis vineyard was raised to grand cru in 1981?
questions.explain: Clos des Lambrays became a grand cru in 1981.

questions.q: Which famous premier cru lies just below Musigny in Chambolle-Musigny?
questions.explain: Les Amoureuses sits just below Musigny. The other three belong to Gevrey, Vosne and Nuits.

questions.q: In which commune do Echezeaux and Grands-Echezeaux lie?
questions.explain: Both lie in Flagey-Echezeaux, whose village wine is sold as Vosne-Romanée.

questions.q: How many grands crus does Nuits-Saint-Georges have?
questions.explain: Nuits-Saint-Georges has no grands crus, only many premiers crus such as Les Saint-Georges.

questions.q: Who built the wall around the Clos de Vougeot?
questions.explain: The Cistercians walled the Clos de Vougeot. Today it is divided among many owners.

questions.q: Which grand cru lies mainly in Chambolle-Musigny, with a small part in Morey-Saint-Denis?
questions.explain: Bonnes-Mares lies at the northern end of Chambolle, and a small part of it lies in Morey.

questions.q: How many grands crus does Gevrey-Chambertin have?
questions.explain: Gevrey has nine grands crus, more than any other village of the Côte de Nuits.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a grand cru of Vosne-Romanée?
questions.explain: Clos de la Roche is a grand cru of Morey-Saint-Denis.

questions.q: Which Vosne-Romanée vineyard became a grand cru in 1992?
questions.explain: La Grande Rue, a monopole, was raised to grand cru in 1992. Cros Parantoux and Les Suchots are premiers crus.

questions.q: Which village can contribute to Côte de Nuits-Villages?
questions.explain: Côte de Nuits-Villages comes from Fixin, Brochon, Premeaux-Prissey, Comblanchien and Corgoloin.

questions.q: Where do Gevrey-Chambertin's grands crus mostly lie?
options: North of the village, towards Fixin
South of the village, towards Morey
On the flat land east of the main road
In the Hautes Côtes behind the village
questions.explain: Most of Gevrey's grands crus lie south of the village, towards Morey-Saint-Denis.

questions.q: Roughly how large is the Clos de Vougeot?

cards.f: Name the six grands crus of Vosne-Romanée.
cards.b: Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, La Romanée, La Grande Rue, Richebourg and Romanée-Saint-Vivant.

Vosne-Romanée monopole that became a grand cru in 1992.

lessons.title: The Côte de Beaune
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the Côte de Beaune from the hill of Corton to the Maranges: Beaune, the red villages of Pommard and Volnay, and the great white villages of Meursault, Puligny and Chassagne.

p: The Côte de Beaune starts at Ladoix-Serrigny. The slope is broader and gentler than in the Côte de Nuits, and much more white wine is made. The hill of Corton is shared by Ladoix, Aloxe-Corton and Pernand-Vergelesses.

Corton is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune and the largest grand cru in Burgundy. Some white Corton is also made. The label may add a climat name, such as Le Clos du Roi, Les Bressandes, Les Renardes or Le Corton.
Corton-Charlemagne is the white grand cru, from Chardonnay on the upper part of the hill, named after the emperor Charlemagne. A separate Charlemagne appellation exists but is almost never used.

Savigny-lès-Beaune and Chorey-lès-Beaune make supple, fruity reds that are often good value. Beaune itself has no grands crus but a large area of premiers crus, including Les Grèves, Les Bressandes, Les Teurons, Clos du Roi and Le Clos des Mouches, which makes both red and white.

The town is the trading heart of Burgundy and home to many négociant houses. The Hospices de Beaune was founded in 1443 by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy. Wine from its vineyards is sold at a charity auction each November.

Pommard and Volnay are both red-only village appellations with no grands crus. Pommard is sturdier and more tannic, with more clay in the soil. Its best premiers crus are Les Rugiens, named after its reddish, iron-rich soil, and Les Grands Epenots and Les Petits Epenots.

Volnay, next door, is lighter and more perfumed, on soils with more limestone. Leading premiers crus are Les Caillerets, Clos des Ducs, Taille Pieds and Clos des Chênes. Red wine from Santenots, which lies in Meursault, is usually sold as Volnay Premier Cru Santenots.
Up a side valley, Monthélie, Auxey-Duresses and Saint-Romain make lighter wines that often offer value.

Meursault is mostly white and has no grands crus. Its wines are rich and rounded, often with hazelnut and butter notes from barrel fermentation and lees ageing. The best premiers crus are Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, with Les Gouttes d'Or and Le Porusot also well known.
The hamlet of Blagny sits above Meursault and Puligny. The Blagny appellation is for red wine. White wine from Blagny is sold as Meursault Premier Cru Blagny or as Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru.

Montrachet straddles Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet. Chevalier-Montrachet lies above it on thinner, stonier soil, and Bâtard-Montrachet below it on deeper soil. Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet lies wholly in Puligny, Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet wholly in Chassagne.

Puligny has a high water table, so few cellars are dug deep. Its whites are precise and fine. Top premiers crus include Les Pucelles, Les Combettes, Les Folatières and Le Cailleret. Chassagne makes both white and red, with premiers crus such as Morgeot, Cailleret, La Romanée and Les Grandes Ruchottes.

Saint-Aubin, behind Puligny and Chassagne, is mostly white. Santenay and Maranges at the southern end are mostly red. Côte de Beaune-Villages is a red wine from the village appellations of the Côte de Beaune except Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, Pommard and Volnay.

key: Corton is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune and the largest grand cru in Burgundy; Corton-Charlemagne is its white partner.
Beaune has no grands crus but many premiers crus; the Hospices de Beaune was founded in 1443.
Pommard and Volnay are red only: Pommard sturdier and more tannic, Volnay lighter and more perfumed.
Meursault has no grands crus; Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes are its leading premiers crus.
Five white grands crus around Montrachet: Montrachet and Bâtard shared, Chevalier and Bienvenues in Puligny, Criots in Chassagne.
Côte de Beaune-Villages is red and excludes Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, Pommard and Volnay.

questions.q: Which is the only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune?

Across the main road on flat land

questions.explain: Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet lies wholly in Puligny. Montrachet and Bâtard are shared, and Criots lies in Chassagne.

questions.q: Who founded the Hospices de Beaune?
options: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy
questions.explain: Nicolas Rolin, chancellor to the Duke of Burgundy, founded the Hospices de Beaune in 1443.

options: Pommard lies higher and is cooler
Volnay is aged without oak by law

questions.explain: Saint-Aubin, behind Puligny and Chassagne, is mostly white. Santenay and Maranges are mostly red.

questions.explain: Beaune, Aloxe-Corton, Pommard and Volnay may not use Côte de Beaune-Villages. Santenay, Saint-Aubin and Monthelie may.

cards.b: From Ladoix-Serrigny in the north to the Maranges in the south.

cards.b: The slope is broader and gentler, and much more white wine is made.
The only red grand cru of the Côte de Beaune and the largest grand cru in Burgundy. Some white is also made.

cards.f: Which three villages share the hill of Corton?
cards.b: Ladoix-Serrigny, Aloxe-Corton and Pernand-Vergelesses.

cards.f: Name some Corton climats that may appear on the label.
cards.b: Le Clos du Roi, Les Bressandes, Les Renardes and Le Corton.
White grand cru from Chardonnay on the upper part of the hill of Corton, named after the emperor Charlemagne.
Villages near Beaune making supple, fruity reds that are often good value.
Les Grèves, Les Bressandes, Les Teurons, Clos du Roi and Le Clos des Mouches, which makes red and white. Beaune has no grands crus.

Red-only village with no grands crus. Sturdier and more tannic than Volnay, on soils with more clay.
Leading Pommard premier cru, named after its reddish, iron-rich soil.
Red-only village with no grands crus. Lighter and more perfumed than Pommard, on soils with more limestone.
Red wine from the Santenots climat, which lies in Meursault, usually sold under the Volnay name.

cards.f: Name the three leading premiers crus of Meursault.
cards.b: Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes.
Hamlet above Meursault and Puligny. Blagny AOC is red. Its white is sold as Meursault or Puligny-Montrachet Premier Cru.

cards.b: Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet and Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet.

cards.f: Why are few cellars dug deep in Puligny-Montrachet?
cards.b: The village has a high water table.
Makes both white and red. Premiers crus include Morgeot, Cailleret, La Romanée and Les Grandes Ruchottes.

lessons.title: Côte Chalonnaise and Mâconnais
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the two southern parts of Burgundy: the five village appellations of the Côte Chalonnaise, and the Mâconnais with Pouilly-Fuissé and its premiers crus, created in 2020.

p: The Côte Chalonnaise lies south of the Maranges and takes its name from the town of Chalon-sur-Saône. Unlike the Côte d'Or it is not one continuous slope. The vineyards sit on scattered hillsides among other farmland.

There are no grands crus, but four of the five village appellations have premiers crus. Bouzeron has none. The wines are usually lighter and ready sooner than those of the Côte d'Or, and often good value. The regional appellations are Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise and, to the west, Bourgogne Côtes du Couchois.

sections.h: Five villages from north to south
p: Bouzeron is the village appellation for Aligoté only. Rully makes more white than red and has a long history of sparkling wine production. Mercurey is the largest village and makes mainly red Pinot Noir.
Givry is also mainly red; tradition says it was a favourite of King Henri IV. Montagny, in the south, is for white wine from Chardonnay only, and a large part of it is classified as premier cru.

The Mâconnais lies further south, around the town of Mâcon on the Saône. It is warmer and sunnier than the Côte d'Or. Most of the wine is white Chardonnay, rounder and riper in fruit than wines further north. Reds are made mostly from Gamay. The village of Chardonnay lies here.

The base appellation is Mâcon. Mâcon followed by a village name, such as Mâcon Davayé or Mâcon Chardonnay, is a step up. Mâcon-Villages is for white wine only. Viré-Clessé and Saint-Véran are village appellations for white wine.

Pouilly-Fuissé lies in the south of the Mâconnais, below the limestone outcrops of the Roche de Solutré and the Roche de Vergisson. It covers four communes: Chaintré, Fuissé, Solutré-Pouilly and Vergisson. It is white only, from Chardonnay, and has more weight and structure than most Mâcon, often with oak ageing.
Its neighbours Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles make similar whites in smaller amounts.

In 2020 Pouilly-Fuissé gained 22 premiers crus, from the 2020 vintage. They were the first premiers crus of the Mâconnais. Among them are Le Clos de Monsieur Noly, Les Crays, Vers Cras, Sur la Roche, Les Perrières, Le Clos Reyssier and Aux Quarts.
The label shows Pouilly-Fuissé Premier Cru with the climat name. Pouilly-Loché and Pouilly-Vinzelles also have a small number of premiers crus, from the 2024 vintage.

key: The Côte Chalonnaise is a broken line of hillsides, not a continuous escarpment; it has premiers crus but no grands crus.
Bouzeron is Aligoté only, Mercurey and Givry are mainly red, Rully more white, Montagny white only.
The Mâconnais is warmer; whites are Chardonnay and reds mostly Gamay. Mâcon-Villages is white only.

Pouilly-Fuissé gained 22 premiers crus in 2020, the first in the Mâconnais.

They must be aged in new oak

paths.title: Bordeaux and the South-West
paths.summary: The geography, grapes, appellations and classifications of Bordeaux, from the Médoc and Graves to Sauternes and the Right Bank, followed by the varied wines of the South-West from Bergerac to Jurançon.

lessons.title: The shape of Bordeaux
lessons.intro: This lesson sets out the map of Bordeaux: its rivers and banks, its maritime climate, the grapes and the logic of blending, the generic appellations that cover the whole region, and the history and trade that shaped it.

p: Bordeaux is the vineyard of the Gironde département in south-west France. Two rivers shape it. The Garonne flows up from the south-east past the city of Bordeaux. The Dordogne flows in from the east. They meet north of the city and form the Gironde, a wide tidal estuary that runs north-west to the Atlantic.

The Left Bank lies west of the Garonne and the Gironde: the Médoc and the Graves. The Right Bank lies north and east of the Dordogne and the Gironde: the Libournais (Saint-Émilion, Pomerol, Fronsac) and further downstream Bourg and Blaye. Between the two rivers is Entre-deux-Mers, 'between two seas', named after the two tidal rivers.

The climate is moderate and maritime. The Atlantic and the Gulf Stream keep winters mild and summers warm rather than hot. To the west, the pine forest of the Landes shelters the vineyards from Atlantic winds. The rivers and estuary also moderate temperatures and lower the risk of frost for vines close to the water.

Rain can fall in any season. Cool, wet weather at flowering causes poor fruit set (coulure and millerandage), and rain near harvest brings rot and dilution. Vintages therefore vary a great deal. Growing several varieties that flower and ripen at different times spreads this risk.

Red Bordeaux is usually a blend. Merlot is the most planted variety: it ripens early and gives soft, plummy, full wines. Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late and gives blackcurrant fruit, firm tannin and acidity, so it needs warm, well-drained sites. Cabernet Franc adds fresh red fruit and fragrance. Petit Verdot, which ripens very late, adds colour and spice in small amounts. Malbec and Carmenère are permitted but now rare.

White Bordeaux is based on Sémillon, which gives body and ages well, and Sauvignon Blanc, which gives aroma and acidity. Muscadelle is a minor, floral partner. The same three grapes make the dry whites of Graves and the sweet wines of Sauternes.

Bordeaux AOC covers the whole region and allows red, rosé, clairet (a darker, fuller rosé from a maceration of a day or two, longer than for most rosé) and dry white. Bordeaux Supérieur, mostly red, has stricter rules such as lower maximum yields and a higher minimum alcohol. Crémant de Bordeaux is traditional method sparkling wine, white or rosé.

Entre-deux-Mers is an appellation for dry white wine only. Reds from the same area are sold as Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur. Côtes de Bordeaux is an umbrella appellation for hillside areas, mostly on the right banks of the rivers. Some areas can add their own name, among them Blaye, Cadillac, Castillon and Francs.

In 1152 Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet, soon King Henry II of England. Bordeaux then belonged to the English crown until 1453, and England became its main market for a light red the English called claret. In the 17th century Dutch engineers drained the marshes of the Médoc, which opened the land where many great estates now stand.

Bordeaux sells through a system known as la Place de Bordeaux. Estates (châteaux) sell to merchants (négociants) through brokers (courtiers), and the négociants sell on to the world. Many leading wines are first offered en primeur, as futures, in the spring after the harvest, long before bottling.

key: The Garonne and the Dordogne meet north of the city to form the Gironde estuary.
Left Bank: Médoc and Graves. Right Bank: Libournais, Bourg and Blaye. Between the rivers: Entre-deux-Mers.
The maritime climate makes vintage variation large; blending varieties that ripen at different times spreads the risk.
Merlot is the most planted grape; Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late and needs warm, well-drained soils.
Entre-deux-Mers AOC is for dry white wine only.

questions.q: Which two rivers meet to form the Gironde estuary?
questions.explain: The Garonne and the Dordogne meet north of the city of Bordeaux and become the Gironde, which flows out to the Atlantic.

questions.q: What does the name Entre-deux-Mers refer to?
options: Two Atlantic bays on either side of the Médoc
The land between the Garonne and the Dordogne, two tidal rivers
The gap between the Gironde and the Landes forest
Two lakes in the south of the Graves
questions.explain: Entre-deux-Mers means 'between two seas' and is the land between the tidal Garonne and Dordogne.

questions.q: What protects the Bordeaux vineyards from Atlantic winds on their western side?
options: The pine forest of the Landes
questions.explain: The large pine forest of the Landes, between the vineyards and the ocean, acts as a windbreak.

questions.q: Why do Bordeaux growers plant several grape varieties rather than one?
options: Only Merlot can be used for rosé
Each variety is legally tied to one bank of the river
Varieties flower and ripen at different times, which spreads weather risk in a maritime climate
questions.explain: Rain at flowering or harvest can hit one variety hard. Grapes that flower and ripen at different times give growers a safety net.

questions.q: Which grape gives Bordeaux blends blackcurrant fruit and firm tannin but ripens late?
questions.explain: Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late and brings structure, acidity and blackcurrant flavour, so it needs warm, well-drained sites.

questions.q: A red wine is made in the Entre-deux-Mers area. Under which appellation can it be sold?
questions.explain: Entre-deux-Mers AOC covers dry white wine only, so reds from the zone use the generic Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérieur appellations.

questions.q: Through whom do Bordeaux châteaux traditionally sell their wine to négociants?
questions.explain: On la Place de Bordeaux, courtiers (brokers) act as intermediaries between the châteaux and the négociants.

questions.q: Which of these is a style allowed under Bordeaux AOC, darker and fuller than a typical rosé?
questions.explain: Clairet is a deeper coloured rosé made with a longer maceration than most rosé, and is part of the generic Bordeaux appellation.

questions.q: In which direction does the Gironde estuary run to the Atlantic?
questions.explain: The Garonne and Dordogne meet north of the city, and the Gironde runs north-west to the ocean.

questions.q: Which grape is the most planted in Bordeaux?
questions.explain: Merlot is the most planted variety. It ripens early and gives soft, full wines.

questions.q: What causes coulure and millerandage in Bordeaux?
questions.explain: Cool, wet weather at flowering leads to poor fruit set, known as coulure and millerandage.

questions.q: Which grape ripens very late and adds colour and spice in small amounts?
questions.explain: Petit Verdot ripens very late and is used in small amounts for colour and spice.

questions.q: Which white grape gives body and ageing potential to white Bordeaux?
questions.explain: Sémillon gives body and ages well. Sauvignon Blanc gives aroma and acidity, and Muscadelle is a minor floral partner.

questions.q: Until which year did Bordeaux belong to the English crown?
questions.explain: Bordeaux came under the English crown after the marriage of 1152 and stayed English until 1453.

questions.q: What does 'en primeur' mean in Bordeaux?
options: Wine sold as futures in the spring after the harvest
questions.explain: Many leading wines are first offered en primeur, as futures, in the spring after the harvest and long before bottling.

questions.q: Who drained the marshes of the Médoc in the 17th century?
questions.explain: Dutch engineers drained the Médoc marshes in the 17th century, opening land where many great estates now stand.

cards.f: Which two rivers form the Gironde estuary?
cards.b: The Garonne and the Dordogne, which meet north of the city of Bordeaux.
West of the Garonne and the Gironde: the Médoc and the Graves.
North and east of the Dordogne and the Gironde: the Libournais, then Bourg and Blaye downstream.
'Between two seas': the land between the tidal Garonne and Dordogne. The appellation is for dry white only.

cards.f: What is the climate of Bordeaux?
cards.b: Moderate and maritime, tempered by the Atlantic and the Gulf Stream. Rain can fall in any season.

cards.f: What shelters Bordeaux from Atlantic winds?
cards.b: The pine forest of the Landes, to the west of the vineyards.
Poor fruit set, caused in Bordeaux by cool, wet weather at flowering.

cards.f: Why are several grape varieties blended in Bordeaux?
cards.b: They flower and ripen at different times, which spreads the weather risk of a maritime climate.
The most planted grape. It ripens early and gives soft, plummy, full wines.
Ripens late and gives blackcurrant fruit, firm tannin and acidity, so it needs warm, well-drained sites.
Adds fresh red fruit and fragrance to the blend.
A very late ripening red grape, used in small amounts for colour and spice. Malbec and Carmenère are also allowed but rare.

cards.f: What are the white grapes of Bordeaux?
cards.b: Sémillon for body and ageing, Sauvignon Blanc for aroma and acidity, and a little Muscadelle.

cards.f: Which six grapes were approved for Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur in 2021?
cards.b: Arinarnoa, Castets, Marselan and Touriga Nacional (red), Alvarinho and Liliorila (white). At most 10% of a blend.
A darker, fuller rosé from a maceration of a day or two, allowed under Bordeaux AOC.
Mostly red generic appellation with stricter rules than Bordeaux, such as lower maximum yields and higher minimum alcohol.
Umbrella appellation for hillside areas, mostly on the right banks. Blaye, Cadillac, Castillon, Francs and Sainte-Foy may add their name.

cards.f: Why did England become the main market for Bordeaux?
cards.b: Eleanor of Aquitaine married Henry Plantagenet in 1152. Bordeaux was English until 1453, and England bought its claret.
The trade system in which châteaux sell to négociants through brokers (courtiers), and négociants sell on to the world.
Sale of wine as futures in the spring after the harvest, long before it is bottled.

lessons.title: The Left Bank: Médoc and the 1855 Classification
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the Médoc peninsula, the gravel soils that suit Cabernet Sauvignon, the four great communes and their neighbours, and the 1855 Classification that still ranks its estates.

p: The Médoc is the peninsula north-west of the city, between the Gironde estuary and the Atlantic pine forest. The vineyards run in a narrow strip along the estuary. The Médoc appellation is used mainly for the northern, lower-lying part, with more clay. Haut-Médoc covers the southern part, nearer the city; 'haut' means upstream, not higher ground.

Inside the Haut-Médoc lie six communal appellations: Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux along the estuary, and Listrac-Médoc and Moulis inland. Haut-Médoc and the six communes are for red wine only. White wines made by Médoc estates are sold as Bordeaux AOC.

The best Médoc soils are deep gravel left by the rivers, often forming low mounds called croupes. Gravel drains freely, keeps the vines on a modest water supply and warms up in the sun, which helps late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon. That is why Cabernet Sauvignon usually leads the blend on the Left Bank.

The finest sites tend to lie close to the estuary, on gravel that slopes gently towards the water. The estuary softens temperature swings. Where clay increases, as in parts of Saint-Estèphe and the northern Médoc, growers plant more Merlot, which copes better with cooler, wetter soils.

Saint-Estèphe is the most northerly commune. It has more clay and gives firm, sturdy wines. Pauillac follows. It holds three first growths, Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild, and is known for powerful wines with blackcurrant and cedar. Saint-Julien, between Pauillac and Margaux, is known for balanced, consistent wines and has no first growth.

Margaux is the southernmost of the great communes. Its appellation spreads over five villages and its thinner gravel gives fragrant, elegant wines. It has more classified growths than any other commune. Inland, away from the estuary, Listrac-Médoc and Moulis have more clay and limestone and no estates in the 1855 Classification.

For the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1855, the Bordeaux Chamber of Commerce asked the city's wine brokers to rank the leading red wines. They based the ranking on the prices the wines had fetched over many years. The result was five tiers, from Premiers Crus (first growths) to Cinquièmes Crus (fifth growths). It classifies châteaux, not plots of land.

All the red wines ranked are from the Médoc except one: Château Haut-Brion in Pessac, in the Graves. The original first growths were Lafite, Latour, Margaux and Haut-Brion. The ranking has changed very little. Cantemerle was added as a fifth growth in 1856, and in 1973 Mouton Rothschild was promoted from second to first growth.

Many Médoc estates are not in the 1855 list. The Cru Bourgeois classification ranks such estates in three levels: Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur and Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel. Unlike 1855, it is reviewed every five years, so estates can move up or down. Many leading châteaux also make a second wine from younger vines or lots not used in the main blend.

key: Haut-Médoc is the southern part of the Médoc, nearer the city; 'haut' means upstream.
The six communal appellations of the Haut-Médoc are Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux, Listrac-Médoc and Moulis, all red only.
Gravel croupes drain well and store heat, ideal for late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon.
The 1855 Classification ranked red wines in five tiers by price, for the Paris Exposition Universelle.
Haut-Brion (Pessac, Graves) is the only red outside the Médoc in the 1855 list; Mouton Rothschild became a first growth in 1973.
Pauillac has three first growths; Margaux has the most classified growths of any commune.

questions.q: What does 'haut' in Haut-Médoc refer to?
options: A higher quality tier fixed in 1855
The upstream part of the peninsula, nearer the city
questions.explain: Haut-Médoc is the southern, upstream part of the Médoc, closer to the city of Bordeaux. The name says nothing about altitude.

questions.q: Which commune is the most northerly of the four great Médoc communes on the estuary?
questions.explain: From north to south the order is Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux.

questions.q: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon do so well on the gravel of the Médoc?
options: Gravel drains freely and warms up, helping a late-ripening variety reach maturity
Gravel holds water, protecting the vines from drought
Gravel is rich in nutrients, which raises yields
Gravel soils delay budbreak and avoid all frost
questions.explain: Free drainage and heat retention help Cabernet Sauvignon, which ripens late, to ripen fully in a maritime climate.

questions.q: On what basis did the brokers rank the wines in the 1855 Classification?
options: The prices the wines had fetched over many years
A blind tasting held in Paris
questions.explain: The brokers drew up the 1855 ranking from the long-term market prices of each château's wine.

questions.q: Which change was made to the first growths of the 1855 Classification in 1973?
options: Mouton Rothschild was promoted from second to first growth
Lafite Rothschild was split into two estates
questions.explain: In 1973 Mouton Rothschild became a first growth, the one major change to the ranking.

questions.q: Which commune holds three of the first growths?
questions.explain: Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild are all in Pauillac.

questions.q: Which two communal appellations lie inland, away from the estuary, with no 1855 classified growths?
questions.explain: Listrac-Médoc and Moulis are the two inland communal appellations of the Haut-Médoc, and neither has an estate in the 1855 list.

questions.q: How does the Cru Bourgeois classification differ from the 1855 Classification?
options: It is reviewed every five years
It ranks vineyards rather than estates
questions.explain: The Cru Bourgeois classification, with three levels, is revised every five years, while the 1855 ranking has barely changed.

questions.q: Which commune has more classified growths than any other in the Médoc?
questions.explain: Margaux, spread over five villages, has the most classified growths of any commune.

questions.q: How many tiers does the 1855 classification of red wines have?
questions.explain: There are five tiers, from Premiers Crus (first growths) to Cinquièmes Crus (fifth growths).

questions.q: Which château was added to the 1855 Classification in 1856?
questions.explain: Cantemerle was added as a fifth growth in 1856. Mouton Rothschild was promoted in 1973.

questions.q: Under which appellation is a dry white wine from a Margaux estate sold?
questions.explain: Margaux, Haut-Médoc and the other Médoc appellations are red only, so Médoc whites are sold as Bordeaux AOC.

questions.q: Which commune lies between Pauillac and Margaux?
questions.explain: From north to south the order is Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux.

questions.q: Which of these was NOT one of the original first growths of 1855?
questions.explain: Mouton Rothschild was a second growth in 1855 and became a first growth in 1973.

questions.q: Why do the finest Médoc sites tend to lie close to the estuary?
options: The soil there is richer in clay
The estuary softens temperature swings, on gravel sloping gently to the water
Only there may vines be irrigated
questions.explain: Gravel slopes near the water drain well, and the estuary softens temperature swings.

questions.q: How many levels does the Cru Bourgeois classification have?
questions.explain: Cru Bourgeois, Cru Bourgeois Supérieur and Cru Bourgeois Exceptionnel.

cards.b: Peninsula north-west of the city, between the Gironde estuary and the Atlantic pine forest. Vines run in a strip along the estuary.

cards.f: How do the Médoc and Haut-Médoc appellations differ?
cards.b: Médoc covers the northern, lower part, with more clay. Haut-Médoc is the southern part; 'haut' means upstream.

cards.f: Name the six communal appellations of the Haut-Médoc.
cards.b: Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux on the estuary, Listrac-Médoc and Moulis inland.

cards.f: What colour are Haut-Médoc and its communal appellations?
cards.b: Red only. White wines from Médoc estates are sold as Bordeaux AOC.
Low mounds of deep river gravel in the Médoc. They drain freely and warm up, which suits Cabernet Sauvignon.

cards.f: Why do Médoc growers plant more Merlot where there is more clay?
cards.b: Merlot copes better with cooler, wetter soils, as in parts of Saint-Estèphe and the northern Médoc.

cards.f: List the four great Médoc communes from north to south.
cards.b: Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien, Margaux.
The most northerly of the great communes. More clay, and firm, sturdy wines.
Home of three first growths: Lafite Rothschild, Latour and Mouton Rothschild. Powerful wines with blackcurrant and cedar.
Between Pauillac and Margaux. Balanced, consistent wines and no first growth.
Southernmost great commune, spread over five villages. Thinner gravel, fragrant wines and the most classified growths.
The two inland communal appellations, with more clay and limestone and no 1855 classified growths.
For the Exposition Universelle in Paris. Brokers ranked the wines by the prices they had fetched over many years.

cards.f: Does the 1855 Classification rank vineyards or châteaux?
cards.b: Châteaux, not plots of land.

cards.f: How many red wines are in the 1855 Classification today?
cards.b: 61: 5 first, 14 second, 14 third, 10 fourth and 18 fifth growths.

cards.f: Name the four original first growths of 1855.
cards.b: Lafite, Latour, Margaux and Haut-Brion.

cards.f: Which 1855 red is not from the Médoc?
cards.b: Château Haut-Brion, in Pessac in the Graves.

cards.f: What changes have been made to the 1855 red classification?
cards.b: Cantemerle was added as a fifth growth in 1856. Mouton Rothschild was promoted from second to first growth in 1973.
Classification of Médoc estates outside 1855, in three levels: Cru Bourgeois, Supérieur and Exceptionnel. Reviewed every five years.
A wine a château makes from younger vines or lots not used in its main blend.

lessons.title: Graves, Pessac-Léognan and Sauternes
lessons.intro: This lesson follows the Left Bank south of the city: the Graves and Pessac-Léognan with their own classification, then the sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac made from grapes affected by noble rot.

p: The Graves runs south-east from the city along the left bank of the Garonne and takes its name from its gravel soils. It is one of the oldest parts of the Bordeaux vineyard. Unlike the Médoc, it is known for both red and dry white wine. Reds blend Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot; whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon.
The Graves appellation covers red and dry white. Graves Supérieures is a separate appellation for sweet white wine. The Sauternes area forms an enclave in the south of the Graves.

Pessac-Léognan was created in 1987 for the northern part of the Graves, partly within the suburbs of Bordeaux. It covers red and dry white wines. The best whites are often fermented and aged in oak and can age for many years.

The Graves Classification was drawn up in 1953 and revised in 1959. It has a single rank, Cru Classé de Graves. Each château is classified for its red, its white or both. All the classified estates lie within what is now Pessac-Léognan. Château Haut-Brion is the only estate that appears in both this classification and the 1855 Classification.

Sauternes lies about 40 km south-east of the city, where the small Ciron river joins the Garonne. The Ciron is cool and the Garonne warmer, so autumn mornings bring mist. Damp mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons favour Botrytis cinerea in its noble form. The fungus pierces the skins, water evaporates, and sugar, acidity and flavour are concentrated.

Noble rot does not spread evenly, so pickers pass through the vineyard several times, picking only affected grapes. These passes are called tries. Yields are very low and some years give little or no sweet wine. Sémillon leads the blend because its thin skin is prone to botrytis, with Sauvignon Blanc for freshness and a little Muscadelle.

The Sauternes appellation covers five communes: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac and Barsac. Barsac also has its own appellation, and its wines may be labelled either Barsac or Sauternes. Good examples taste of honey, apricot and marmalade, with acidity that keeps them fresh for decades.

The 1855 Classification also ranked the sweet white wines of Sauternes and Barsac. Château d'Yquem, in Sauternes, stands alone as Premier Cru Supérieur. Below it come the Premiers Crus and then the Deuxièmes Crus.

sections.h: Other sweet wines of the Garonne
p: Cérons, inside the Graves just north of Barsac, makes sweet white wine in a similar way. Across the Garonne, on its right bank, Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont also make sweet whites from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle. They face Sauternes across the river and are usually lighter and less concentrated.

key: The Graves is named after its gravel and makes both red and dry white wines.
Pessac-Léognan, the northern Graves, became an appellation in 1987.
The Graves Classification (1953, revised 1959) has one rank, Cru Classé de Graves, for red, white or both.
Haut-Brion is in both the 1855 and the Graves classifications.
In Sauternes, mist from the cool Ciron meeting the Garonne encourages noble rot; grapes are picked in several tries.
In the 1855 sweet wine ranking, Château d'Yquem is the only Premier Cru Supérieur.

questions.q: When was the Pessac-Léognan appellation created?
questions.explain: Pessac-Léognan was carved out of the northern Graves in 1987. 1953 and 1959 are the dates of the Graves Classification.

questions.q: How many ranks does the Graves Classification have?
options: Two: Premier Cru and Deuxième Cru
questions.explain: The Graves Classification has a single rank. Each château is listed for its red, its white or both.

questions.q: Which estate appears in both the 1855 Classification and the Graves Classification?
questions.explain: Haut-Brion, in Pessac, was ranked a first growth in 1855 and is also a Cru Classé de Graves.

questions.q: What local feature encourages noble rot in Sauternes?
options: Morning mists where the cool Ciron meets the warmer Garonne
Heavy summer rain from the Atlantic
questions.explain: The cool Ciron meeting the warmer Garonne creates autumn morning mist; dry afternoons then let botrytis develop in its noble form.

questions.q: Why is Sémillon the main grape of Sauternes?
options: It ripens latest of all Bordeaux grapes
It is the only white grape allowed
Its thin skin makes it prone to noble rot
It has the highest natural acidity
questions.explain: Sémillon's thin skin lets botrytis take hold. Sauvignon Blanc is added for acidity and freshness.

questions.q: In Sauternes, what are 'tries'?
options: Successive passes through the vineyard to pick only botrytised grapes
Tasting panels that approve each vintage
questions.explain: Because noble rot spreads unevenly, pickers make several passes, called tries, to harvest only affected grapes.

questions.q: How may a sweet wine from Barsac be labelled?
questions.explain: Barsac is one of the five communes of Sauternes and also has its own appellation, so producers may use either name.

questions.q: Which sweet wine appellations face Sauternes from the right bank of the Garonne?
questions.explain: Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont lie across the Garonne from Sauternes. Cérons is on the same side as Sauternes.

questions.q: Which grape varieties may be used in Sauternes?
options: Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Petit Manseng
Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle
questions.explain: The Sauternes specification allows Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle. Sémillon leads the blend.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five communes of the Sauternes appellation?
questions.explain: Sauternes covers Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac and Barsac. Cérons is a separate appellation to the north.

questions.q: How many châteaux are in the Graves Classification?
questions.explain: The Graves Classification lists 16 châteaux, all now in Pessac-Léognan. 61 is the 1855 red list and 27 the 1855 sweet list.

questions.q: What does noble rot do to the grapes?
options: It adds colour to the skins
It turns the whole bunch to grey rot
It pierces the skins, so water evaporates and sugar, acidity and flavour concentrate
It stops the grapes ripening early
questions.explain: In its noble form Botrytis pierces the skins. Water evaporates and sugar, acidity and flavour are concentrated.

questions.q: When was the Graves Classification drawn up?
questions.explain: The Graves Classification dates from 1953 and was revised in 1959. Pessac-Léognan was created in 1987.

questions.q: Graves Supérieures is an appellation for which style?
questions.explain: Graves covers red and dry white. Graves Supérieures is a separate appellation for sweet white wine.

questions.q: Where does Cérons lie?
options: On the right bank of the Garonne, next to Loupiac
Inside the Graves, just north of Barsac
questions.explain: Cérons lies inside the Graves on the left bank, just north of Barsac.

questions.q: Why do some vintages give little or no Sauternes?
options: The rules allow it only one year in three
The vines are replanted every few years
Noble rot may not develop well, and yields are very low
Growers must sell the grapes for dry white
questions.explain: Noble rot spreads unevenly and depends on the weather. Yields are very low, so poor autumns give little sweet wine.

cards.b: South-east of the city on the left bank of the Garonne, named after its gravel. Makes red and dry white.

cards.f: What are the usual blends in the Graves?
cards.b: Reds blend Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon.
A separate appellation for sweet white wine from the Graves.
Appellation created in 1987 for the northern Graves, partly in the suburbs of Bordeaux. Red and dry white.
Drawn up in 1953 and revised in 1959. One rank, Cru Classé de Graves, given for red, white or both.

cards.f: How many châteaux are in the Graves Classification?
cards.b: 16, all within what is now Pessac-Léognan.

cards.f: Which estate is in both the 1855 and the Graves classifications?
cards.b: Château Haut-Brion, in Pessac.
Small, cool river that joins the warmer Garonne at Sauternes, causing the autumn mists that favour noble rot.
A fungus that pierces grape skins after misty mornings and dry afternoons, concentrating sugar, acidity and flavour.
Successive passes through the vineyard to pick only botrytised grapes. Sauternes must be picked by hand.

cards.f: Why is Sémillon the main grape of Sauternes?
cards.b: Its thin skin is prone to noble rot. Sauvignon Blanc adds freshness, with a little Muscadelle.

cards.f: Name the five communes of the Sauternes appellation.
cards.b: Sauternes, Bommes, Fargues, Preignac and Barsac.
Commune with its own appellation inside the Sauternes area. Its sweet wines may be labelled Barsac or Sauternes.

cards.f: What is the maximum yield for Sauternes?
cards.b: 25 hl/ha. Some years give little or no sweet wine.

cards.f: What sugar levels does Sauternes require?
cards.b: Grapes with at least 221 g/l of sugar, and at least 45 g/l of sugar left in the finished wine.

cards.f: What does good Sauternes taste of?
cards.b: Honey, apricot and marmalade, with acidity that keeps it fresh for decades.
In Sauternes, the only Premier Cru Supérieur in the 1855 classification of sweet wines.

cards.f: How is the 1855 sweet wine classification structured today?
cards.b: 1 Premier Cru Supérieur, 11 Premiers Crus and 15 Deuxièmes Crus, from Sauternes and Barsac.
Sweet white appellation inside the Graves, just north of Barsac.
Sweet whites from the right bank of the Garonne, facing Sauternes. Usually lighter and less concentrated.

lessons.title: The Right Bank: Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and Fronsac
lessons.intro: This lesson crosses the Dordogne to the Libournais, where Merlot and Cabernet Franc grow on clay and limestone. It covers Saint-Émilion and its classification, Pomerol, Fronsac, the satellites and the other Right Bank areas.

sections.h: Merlot and Cabernet Franc on clay and limestone
p: The Libournais is named after Libourne, the river port where the Isle joins the Dordogne. Its soils hold more clay and limestone than the Médoc gravels. Clay stays cool and holds water, which suits early-ripening Merlot. Cabernet Franc, known locally as Bouchet, does well on limestone and gives freshness and fragrance.

Cabernet Sauvignon plays a small role here, because it ripens late and struggles on cool soils. Right Bank reds are therefore Merlot-led blends, often softer and rounder in their youth than Left Bank reds.

sections.h: Saint-Émilion: town, soils and two appellations
p: Saint-Émilion is a medieval hill town whose surrounding jurisdiction is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Around the town lies a limestone plateau, edged by steep clay-limestone slopes called the côtes. Below are sandier soils towards the Dordogne, and in the north-west, by the Pomerol border, a zone of gravel.

Two appellations share the same area. Saint-Émilion AOC is the basic one. Saint-Émilion Grand Cru AOC has stricter rules, such as lower maximum yields. 'Grand Cru' on its own is therefore an appellation, not a rank. Across the Barbanne stream to the north lie four satellites: Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges.

Saint-Émilion has its own classification, first published in 1955 and intended to be revised about every ten years. Only wines of the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation can be classified. There are three ranks: Premier Grand Cru Classé A, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and Grand Cru Classé. Châteaux apply and are judged on tastings of several vintages and on other criteria.

Because the list is revised, estates can be promoted or demoted, and some have chosen to leave the classification. Results have been challenged in court more than once. The list of châteaux in each rank changes, so always check the current edition instead of learning a fixed list.

Pomerol is a small, gently sloping plateau north-east of Libourne, bordering Saint-Émilion. Its soils mix gravel, sand and clay, and at the highest point a dense clay subsoil underlies the most famous estate, Petrus. Merlot dominates, giving rich, plush wines. Estates are small and often lack the grand château buildings of the Médoc.

Pomerol has no official classification. Prestige rests on reputation and price alone. The appellation is for red wine only. Lalande-de-Pomerol lies just north, across the Barbanne stream, and makes similar Merlot-based reds.

sections.h: Fronsac and the wider Right Bank
p: Fronsac lies west of Libourne, on hills of clay and limestone above the Dordogne and the Isle. Canon Fronsac is a smaller appellation within it, on the slopes. Both make Merlot-led reds, often firmer than those of Pomerol.

Further downstream, Bourg and Blaye face the Médoc across the Gironde and make mainly Merlot-based reds. East of Saint-Émilion, Castillon and Francs are part of the Côtes de Bordeaux, on similar clay and limestone.

key: Right Bank reds are led by Merlot, with Cabernet Franc (Bouchet); cool clay suits Merlot.
Saint-Émilion and Saint-Émilion Grand Cru are two appellations over the same area; Grand Cru has stricter rules.
The Saint-Émilion classification (first 1955) applies only to Grand Cru wines and is revised periodically.
Its three ranks are Premier Grand Cru Classé A, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and Grand Cru Classé.
Pomerol has no official classification; its wines are Merlot-dominated and red only.
Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges are the Saint-Émilion satellites north of the Barbanne.

questions.q: Why does Merlot dominate on the Right Bank?
options: It is the only red grape allowed there
It ripens early and suits the cool, water-retentive clay soils
It needs hot gravel to ripen
It resists noble rot better than other grapes
questions.explain: Merlot ripens early and thrives on cool clay, where late-ripening Cabernet Sauvignon struggles.

questions.q: What is the local name for Cabernet Franc in Saint-Émilion?
questions.explain: Cabernet Franc is called Bouchet on the Right Bank. Côt and Auxerrois are names for Malbec, Mansois for Fer Servadou.

questions.q: A label reads 'Saint-Émilion Grand Cru'. What does this tell you?
options: The wine comes from the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation, which has stricter rules
The château is a Premier Grand Cru Classé A
The wine is from the Pomerol border gravels
The château is in the 1855 Classification
questions.explain: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation. Only a 'Grand Cru Classé' or 'Premier Grand Cru Classé' is ranked in the classification.

questions.q: Which wines are eligible for the Saint-Émilion classification?
options: Wines from the four satellite appellations
Wines of the Saint-Émilion AOC only
Wines of the Saint-Émilion Grand Cru appellation only
questions.explain: Only châteaux producing Saint-Émilion Grand Cru can be classified.

questions.q: What is the top rank of the Saint-Émilion classification?
questions.explain: The ranks are Premier Grand Cru Classé A, then B, then Grand Cru Classé. Premier Cru Supérieur is Château d'Yquem's rank in 1855.

questions.q: How are the leading estates of Pomerol officially classified?
options: They are not: Pomerol has no official classification
questions.explain: Pomerol has never had an official classification. Its reputation rests on the wines and their prices.

questions.q: Which stream separates Saint-Émilion and Pomerol from their northern neighbours such as Montagne and Lalande-de-Pomerol?
questions.explain: The Barbanne stream runs to the north, with the Saint-Émilion satellites and Lalande-de-Pomerol beyond it.

questions.q: Where is Fronsac?
options: On the Left Bank, south of Margaux
Inside the Graves, next to Pessac
Across the Gironde from the Médoc, next to Blaye
West of Libourne, on clay-limestone hills above the Dordogne and the Isle
questions.explain: Fronsac and Canon Fronsac sit on hills west of Libourne, where the Isle meets the Dordogne.

questions.q: Which river port gives the Libournais its name?
questions.explain: Libourne is the river port where the Isle joins the Dordogne.

questions.q: Where are Bourg and Blaye?
options: Facing the Médoc across the Gironde
North of Pomerol across the Barbanne
questions.explain: Bourg and Blaye lie downstream on the Right Bank, facing the Médoc across the Gironde.

questions.q: What soil lies in the north-west of Saint-Émilion, by the Pomerol border?
questions.explain: The north-west of Saint-Émilion, next to Pomerol, has a zone of gravel.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a Saint-Émilion satellite?
questions.explain: The satellites are Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges. Lalande-de-Pomerol is Pomerol's northern neighbour.

questions.q: Which wines may the Pomerol appellation produce?
questions.explain: Pomerol is an appellation for red wine only.

questions.q: In which year was the Saint-Émilion classification first published?
questions.explain: The first Saint-Émilion classification was published in 1955.

questions.q: Why are Right Bank reds often softer and rounder in youth than Left Bank reds?
options: They are led by Merlot rather than Cabernet Sauvignon
questions.explain: Right Bank blends are Merlot-led. Merlot gives softer, rounder wines than Cabernet Sauvignon.

questions.q: What are the côtes of Saint-Émilion?
options: Steep clay-limestone slopes edging the plateau
Terraces on the banks of the Garonne
questions.explain: The côtes are the steep clay-limestone slopes around the limestone plateau of Saint-Émilion.

cards.b: Right Bank area named after Libourne, the port where the Isle joins the Dordogne: Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and Fronsac.

cards.f: Why does Merlot suit the Right Bank?
cards.b: It ripens early and thrives on cool, water-retaining clay.
The Right Bank name for Cabernet Franc, which does well on limestone and gives freshness and fragrance.

cards.f: Why does Cabernet Sauvignon play a small role on the Right Bank?
cards.b: It ripens late and struggles on the cool clay and limestone soils.

cards.f: What are the main soils of Saint-Émilion?
cards.b: A limestone plateau edged by clay-limestone côtes, sandier soils towards the Dordogne, and gravel by Pomerol.
The steep clay-limestone slopes around the edge of the limestone plateau.

cards.f: When was the Jurisdiction of Saint-Émilion listed by UNESCO?
cards.b: In 1999, the first vineyard landscape on the World Heritage list. It covers eight villages.
Two appellations over the same area. Grand Cru has stricter rules, such as lower yields. It is not a rank.
First published in 1955 and revised about every ten years. Only Saint-Émilion Grand Cru wines can be classified.

cards.f: What are the ranks of the Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.b: Premier Grand Cru Classé A, Premier Grand Cru Classé B and Grand Cru Classé.

cards.f: How are châteaux judged for the Saint-Émilion classification?
cards.b: On tastings of several vintages and other criteria. Estates can be promoted or demoted, and some have left.
Montagne, Lussac, Puisseguin and Saint-Georges, north of the Barbanne stream.
Stream north of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, with the satellites and Lalande-de-Pomerol beyond it.
Small, gently sloping plateau north-east of Libourne, on gravel, sand and clay. Merlot dominates. Red only.

cards.f: What lies beneath Petrus, at the highest point of Pomerol?
cards.b: A dense clay subsoil.

cards.f: Does Pomerol have an official classification?
cards.b: No. Its prestige rests on reputation and price alone.
Just north of Pomerol across the Barbanne, making similar Merlot-based reds.
West of Libourne, on clay-limestone hills above the Dordogne and the Isle. Canon Fronsac is a smaller area on the slopes.
Right Bank areas facing the Médoc across the Gironde, making mainly Merlot-based reds.
Côtes de Bordeaux areas east of Saint-Émilion, on similar clay and limestone.

lessons.title: The South-West
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the South-West (Sud-Ouest), the scattered vineyards between Bordeaux and the Pyrenees. Some use Bordeaux grapes, others local ones such as Malbec, Tannat and the Mansengs. Key areas are Bergerac and Monbazillac, Cahors, Madiran and Jurançon.

p: The South-West is not one block but a set of separate vineyard areas along the rivers that flow towards Bordeaux, and in the foothills of the Pyrenees. For centuries these upriver wines had to wait until Bordeaux had sold its own before they could be shipped from its port, which held back their trade.

Close to Bordeaux, in Bergerac, Côtes de Duras, Côtes du Marmandais and Buzet, the grapes are mainly the Bordeaux varieties. Further inland and south, local grapes take over: Malbec in Cahors, Tannat in Madiran, Négrette in Fronton, Fer Servadou in Marcillac and Gaillac, and Gros and Petit Manseng in Jurançon.

Bergerac lies on the Dordogne, upstream of Saint-Émilion. It makes red, rosé and white wines from Bordeaux varieties. Côtes de Bergerac has stricter rules. Pécharmant, on slopes north-east of the town, makes reds, and Rosette makes lightly sweet whites. In Montravel, to the west, Montravel is known for dry whites, while Côtes de Montravel and Haut-Montravel make sweet ones.

Monbazillac lies on the south bank of the Dordogne opposite Bergerac. It makes sweet white wine from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle, concentrated by noble rot as in Sauternes. Saussignac, to the west, also makes sweet whites.

Cahors lies in the valley of the Lot. Its red wines must contain at least 70% Malbec, known locally as Côt or Auxerrois, with Merlot and Tannat making up the rest. Vines grow on terraces along the river and on the limestone plateau (causse) above. Cahors was long called the 'black wine' for its deep colour. The appellation is for red wine only.

Further east, Gaillac on the Tarn uses local grapes such as Mauzac, Len de l'El, Braucol (Fer Servadou) and Duras, in many styles including sparkling wine made by the méthode ancestrale. Fronton, north of Toulouse, is based on Négrette. Marcillac makes reds mostly from Fer Servadou, called Mansois there.

Madiran, in Gascony, makes red wine based on Tannat, a grape with very high tannin and deep colour. It is often blended with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon or Fer. Young Madiran can be hard, and the technique of micro-oxygenation was developed here in the 1990s to soften its tannins.

Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh covers the same area for white wines, dry or sweet, from Gros Manseng, Petit Manseng, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac. Saint-Mont, next door, also uses Tannat. In the French Basque Country, Irouléguy makes mostly Tannat-based reds on steep mountain slopes.

Jurançon lies in the Pyrenean foothills near Pau. Its grapes are Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng. Sweet Jurançon is mostly made by passerillage: grapes are left on the vine late into autumn, where dry, sunny weather shrivels them and concentrates sugar. Noble rot is not the main method. Petit Manseng, with small, thick-skinned berries, suits this well.
The Mansengs keep high acidity, so sweet Jurançon tastes fresh and lively, with flavours of tropical fruit and spice. Jurançon sec is the dry version, usually led by Gros Manseng.

key: Bergerac, Côtes de Duras, Côtes du Marmandais and Buzet mainly use the Bordeaux grape varieties.
Monbazillac, opposite Bergerac on the Dordogne, makes sweet white wine from noble-rotted grapes.
Cahors reds must contain at least 70% Malbec (Côt, Auxerrois), with Merlot and Tannat.
Madiran is based on Tannat; micro-oxygenation was developed there to soften its tannins.
Sweet Jurançon is made mainly by passerillage of Petit and Gros Manseng, not by noble rot.
Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh is the white wine (dry or sweet) of the Madiran area.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Malbec in a Cahors red?
questions.explain: Cahors must contain at least 70% Malbec, with Merlot and Tannat allowed for the rest.

questions.q: Which grape is the basis of Madiran?
questions.explain: Madiran is built on Tannat, a deeply coloured and very tannic variety.

questions.q: How is sweet Jurançon mainly made?
options: By passerillage: grapes shrivel on the vine in dry autumn weather
By noble rot encouraged by river mists
By adding grape spirit during fermentation
By freezing the grapes on the vine
questions.explain: Jurançon relies mostly on passerillage, the drying of late-harvested Manseng grapes on the vine, rather than on botrytis.

questions.q: Which appellation lies opposite Bergerac and makes sweet whites from noble-rotted grapes?
questions.explain: Monbazillac, on the south bank of the Dordogne, makes botrytised sweet whites from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle.

questions.q: Which appellation makes the white wines, dry or sweet, of the Madiran area?
questions.explain: Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh covers the same zone as Madiran but for whites from the Mansengs, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac.

questions.q: What technique was developed in Madiran in the 1990s to soften Tannat?
questions.explain: Micro-oxygenation, the controlled addition of small amounts of oxygen, was developed in Madiran to tame Tannat's tannins.

questions.q: Which grapes are used in Bergerac?
questions.explain: Bergerac, on the Dordogne upstream of Saint-Émilion, uses Merlot, the Cabernets, Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and the other Bordeaux grapes.

questions.q: Fronton, north of Toulouse, is known for which local red grape?
questions.explain: Fronton is based on Négrette. Mansois is Fer Servadou in Marcillac, and Len de l'El is a white grape of Gaillac.

questions.q: On which river does Cahors lie?
questions.explain: Cahors lies in the valley of the Lot, with vines on terraces and on the causse above.

questions.q: Which South-West appellation lies in the French Basque Country?
questions.explain: Irouléguy makes mostly Tannat-based reds on steep mountain slopes in the Basque Country.

questions.q: Which grapes make Jurançon?
questions.explain: Jurançon is made from Petit and Gros Manseng.

questions.q: Which appellation near Bergerac makes red wine on slopes north-east of the town?
questions.explain: Pécharmant makes reds. Rosette makes lightly sweet whites, Saussignac sweet whites and Montravel mostly dry whites.

questions.q: On which river does Gaillac lie?
questions.explain: Gaillac lies on the Tarn, east of the Bordeaux-influenced areas.

questions.q: Why does sweet Jurançon taste fresh in spite of its sugar?
options: It is fortified with grape spirit
It is made from noble-rotted Sémillon
questions.explain: Petit and Gros Manseng keep high acidity, so sweet Jurançon tastes fresh and lively.

questions.q: Which method is used for some sparkling Gaillac?
questions.explain: Gaillac makes sparkling wine by the méthode ancestrale, among its many styles.

questions.q: Which wines may the Cahors appellation produce?
questions.explain: Cahors is an appellation for red wine only.

cards.f: Why was the South-West wine trade long held back?
cards.b: Upriver wines had to wait until Bordeaux had sold its own before they could be shipped from its port.

cards.f: Which South-West areas mainly use the Bordeaux grapes?
cards.b: Bergerac, Côtes de Duras, Côtes du Marmandais and Buzet.
On the Dordogne, upstream of Saint-Émilion. Red, rosé and white from Bordeaux varieties.
Red wine appellation on slopes north-east of Bergerac.

cards.f: What do Montravel, Côtes de Montravel and Haut-Montravel make?
cards.b: Montravel is known for dry whites. Côtes de Montravel and Haut-Montravel make sweet whites.
On the south bank of the Dordogne opposite Bergerac. Sweet whites from noble-rotted Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle.
Sweet white appellation to the west of Monbazillac.
Red only, in the Lot valley. At least 70% Malbec, called Côt or Auxerrois, with Merlot and Tannat.
On terraces along the Lot and on the limestone plateau above it, the causse.

cards.f: Why was Cahors called the black wine?
cards.b: Because of its very deep colour.
On the Tarn. Local grapes such as Mauzac, Len de l'El, Braucol (Fer Servadou) and Duras, in many styles.
The main red grape of Fronton, north of Toulouse.
The name for Fer Servadou in Marcillac, where it makes most of the red wine.
Red only, in Gascony. Based on Tannat, often blended with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon or Fer.
Very tannic, deeply coloured grape. Besides Madiran it is used in Saint-Mont and in Basque Irouléguy.
Controlled addition of small amounts of oxygen to wine, developed in Madiran in the 1990s to soften Tannat.
White wine, dry or sweet, from the Madiran area: Gros and Petit Manseng, Petit Courbu and Arrufiac.
In the Pyrenean foothills near Pau. Sweet and dry whites from Petit and Gros Manseng. Jurançon sec is usually Gros Manseng led.
Grapes left on the vine to shrivel in dry autumn weather. It, not noble rot, makes most sweet Jurançon.

cards.f: Why does Petit Manseng suit sweet Jurançon?
cards.b: Its small, thick-skinned berries shrivel well on the vine and keep high acidity.

paths.title: Champagne, Alsace and the Loire
paths.summary: The cool northern half of French wine: Champagne's districts, grapes and traditional method, Alsace and its grands crus and sweet wines, and the Loire from Muscadet to Sancerre.

lessons.title: Champagne: region and grapes
lessons.intro: This lesson covers where Champagne is, why its cool climate and chalk matter, the four main districts and the grapes grown in each. It also explains the village classification and the codes that tell you who made the wine.

p: Champagne lies east of Paris, around the towns of Reims and Épernay. Most vineyards are in the Marne department, with the Aube to the south and smaller areas in the Aisne and elsewhere. It is one of the most northerly quality wine regions of France.

The climate is cool, with both oceanic and continental influences. Grapes ripen slowly and keep high acidity, which suits sparkling wine. Spring frost, hail and rain at harvest are regular risks, so quality and quantity vary from year to year. Blending across villages, grapes and vintages evens out these differences.

Much of the Marne sits on chalk. Chalk drains well but is porous: it holds water and releases it to the vine roots in dry spells. The purest form, belemnite chalk, lies under many of the best slopes. The chalk also allowed the digging of the deep cellars, called crayères, where wine ages at a cool, steady temperature.

Not all of Champagne is chalk. The Vallée de la Marne has more clay, marl and sand. The Côte des Bar in the Aube sits on Kimmeridgian marl, the same soil as Chablis, which lies closer to it than Reims does.

The Montagne de Reims is a wooded plateau between Reims and Épernay. Its slopes face many directions, some even north, as at Verzenay. Pinot Noir dominates and gives structure and body. The Vallée de la Marne runs west from Épernay. Its cooler, frost-prone valley sites are planted mainly with Meunier, though Aÿ at its eastern end is famous for Pinot Noir.

The Côte des Blancs is an east-facing slope south of Épernay, planted almost entirely with Chardonnay. Villages such as Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger give fine, long-lived wines. The Côte des Bar, far to the south in the Aube, is mostly Pinot Noir and gives riper, fruitier wines.

Seven grapes are allowed, but three make almost all Champagne. Pinot Noir brings body, red fruit and structure. Meunier buds late and ripens early, so it avoids spring frost and suits cool, low-lying sites. It gives fruity, supple wines that are ready sooner. Chardonnay brings finesse, citrus, high acidity and long ageing.

The four minor grapes are Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Arbane and Petit Meslier. They are rare but some producers use them in special cuvées. A disease-resistant variety, Voltis, is now also allowed in small amounts under a trial scheme. Grapes must be picked as whole bunches, which in practice means by hand, so black grapes can give clear juice.

Champagne ranks whole villages, not single vineyards. Under the échelle des crus, each village had a percentage that once set the price of its grapes. That price system has ended, but the terms remain: 17 villages are grand cru, such as Ambonnay, Bouzy, Aÿ, Avize and Cramant, and a larger group are premier cru.

Labels carry a code for the type of producer. NM (négociant manipulant) is a house that buys grapes, as most large houses do. RM (récoltant manipulant) is a grower who makes wine only from their own vineyards. CM (coopérative de manipulation) is a cooperative. Champagne received its AOC in 1936.

key: Champagne is cool and marginal: high acidity, variable vintages, and blending to even them out.
Chalk drains well yet stores water; the Côte des Bar has Kimmeridgian marl like Chablis.
Montagne de Reims: Pinot Noir. Vallée de la Marne: Meunier. Côte des Blancs: Chardonnay. Côte des Bar (Aube): Pinot Noir.
Seven traditional grapes are allowed; Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay dominate. Whole-bunch picking means hand harvesting.
17 villages are grand cru under the échelle des crus.
NM is a house that buys grapes, RM a grower using only its own fruit, CM a cooperative.

questions.q: Which grape is planted most widely in the Vallée de la Marne?
questions.explain: Meunier dominates the Vallée de la Marne because it buds late and ripens early, which suits the cooler, frost-prone valley sites.

questions.q: What soil is typical of the Côte des Bar?
questions.explain: The Côte des Bar in the Aube sits on Kimmeridgian marl, the same soil as nearby Chablis, rather than the chalk of the Marne.

questions.q: Which grape is planted almost exclusively on the Côte des Blancs?
questions.explain: The Côte des Blancs takes its name from its white grape, Chardonnay, which covers almost all of the slope.

questions.q: Why is chalk valued in Champagne's vineyards?
options: It drains well but stores water and releases it to the roots in dry spells
It is rich in organic matter and supports high yields
It is dark and absorbs heat, helping grapes ripen
It stops vines from rooting deeply, which lowers acidity
questions.explain: Chalk is free-draining yet porous, so it holds a reserve of water that the vine can draw on when the weather is dry.

questions.q: How many villages are classified grand cru under the échelle des crus?
questions.explain: Seventeen villages are grand cru, among them Ambonnay, Bouzy, Aÿ, Avize and Cramant.

questions.q: Why does Meunier suit the cooler, low-lying sites of Champagne?
options: It has the highest natural acidity of the three main grapes
It gives the most structured, long-lived base wines
It is the only grape that can be machine harvested
It buds late and ripens early, avoiding spring frost and fitting a short season
questions.explain: Late budding protects Meunier from spring frost, and early ripening lets it reach maturity in cool sites.

questions.q: What does the code RM on a Champagne label mean?
options: A house that buys grapes from growers
A cooperative that makes and sells wine
A grower who makes wine only from their own vineyards
A merchant who buys finished wine and adds a label
questions.explain: RM stands for récoltant manipulant: a grower who makes and sells Champagne from their own grapes.

questions.q: In which department does the Côte des Bar lie?
questions.explain: The Côte des Bar is in the Aube, far to the south of Reims and Épernay in the Marne.

questions.q: Which of these grand cru villages lies on the Côte des Blancs?
questions.explain: Le Mesnil-sur-Oger is a Chardonnay grand cru on the Côte des Blancs. Bouzy and Verzenay are on the Montagne de Reims and Aÿ is in the Vallée de la Marne.

questions.q: Which district lies south of the Côte des Blancs and is planted mainly with Chardonnay?
questions.explain: The Côte de Sézanne continues south of the Côte des Blancs and is mostly Chardonnay. The Côte des Bar, much further south, is mostly Pinot Noir.

questions.q: Which of these grapes is NOT permitted for Champagne?
questions.explain: Arbane, Petit Meslier and Pinot Blanc are among the four minor Champagne grapes. Sauvignon Blanc is not allowed.

questions.q: What is the largest share of a Champagne blend that Voltis may make up?
questions.explain: Voltis may make up at most 10% of a blend and may not be used alone. Growers may plant it on up to 5% of their vineyards.

questions.q: On the old échelle des crus, what rating did a grand cru village have?
questions.explain: Grand cru villages were rated 100%. Premier cru villages were rated 90 to 99%.

questions.q: Which district is known for Pinot Noir and has some north-facing slopes, as at Verzenay?
questions.explain: The Montagne de Reims has slopes facing many directions. Pinot Noir dominates there.

questions.q: What does RC on a Champagne label mean?
options: A grower who sells Champagne made by a cooperative under their own label
A house that buys grapes from growers
A brand owned by a retailer
A cooperative selling under its own name
questions.explain: RC is récoltant coopérateur. A house that buys grapes is NM, a retailer's brand is MA and a cooperative is CM.

questions.q: Which pruning system may be used only for Meunier in Champagne?
questions.explain: The Vallée de la Marne system is reserved for Meunier. Chablis, Cordon de Royat and Guyot may be used more widely.

cards.b: Reims and Épernay, east of Paris.

cards.f: When did Champagne become an AOC, and when was it listed by UNESCO?
cards.b: AOC in 1936. Its hillsides, houses and cellars became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015.
The purest chalk of the Marne, under many of the best slopes. It drains well and stores water for the roots.
Deep cellars dug in the chalk, where wine ages at a cool, steady temperature.

cards.f: Soil of the Côte des Bar
cards.b: Kimmeridgian marl, the same soil as Chablis, rather than the chalk of the Marne.
A wooded plateau between Reims and Épernay with slopes facing many ways. Pinot Noir dominates and gives body.
A Montagne de Reims grand cru with some north-facing slopes, known for Pinot Noir.
Runs west from Épernay. Its cool, frost-prone valley sites are planted mainly with Meunier.
A grand cru at the eastern end of the Vallée de la Marne, famous for Pinot Noir.
An east-facing slope south of Épernay, almost all Chardonnay. Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger are grands crus.
A district south of the Côte des Blancs, planted mainly with Chardonnay.

cards.f: What does each main grape bring to Champagne?
cards.b: Pinot Noir: body and structure. Meunier: fruit and suppleness. Chardonnay: finesse, acidity and ageing.

cards.f: Why does Meunier suit cool valley sites?
cards.b: It buds late and ripens early, so it avoids spring frost and ripens in a short season.
Pinot Blanc, Pinot Gris, Arbane and Petit Meslier.
A disease-resistant grape allowed under a trial scheme: up to 5% of a holding and at most 10% of a blend.
As whole bunches, which in practice means by hand, so black grapes can give clear juice.
The old village ranking that set grape prices. Grand cru villages were rated 100% and premier cru villages 90 to 99%.

cards.f: How many grand cru and premier cru villages?
cards.b: 17 grand cru and 42 premier cru villages.
Chablis, Cordon de Royat, Guyot and Vallée de la Marne, the last for Meunier only.
NM: a house that buys grapes. RM: a grower using only its own grapes. CM: a cooperative. RC: a grower selling co-op wine under its own label.

lessons.title: Champagne: method and styles
lessons.intro: This lesson follows a bottle of Champagne from pressing to dosage. It covers the traditional method, the legal ageing minimums, the sweetness scale, the main styles and the two still-wine appellations of the region.

p: Grapes are pressed gently, as whole bunches. From 4,000 kg of grapes, the press may yield 2,550 litres of juice. The first 2,050 litres, the cuvée, are the finest. The last 500 litres, the taille, are fruitier and less fine. The juice ferments into a dry, high-acid still wine, the vin clair.

The base wines are then blended. This assemblage brings together grapes, villages and often years. Houses keep reserve wines from earlier harvests to give a non-vintage blend its consistent house style from year to year.
