Carthusian monks founded the monastery of Scala Dei here in the 12th century and planted vines. After phylloxera the region declined. In the late 1980s a small group including René Barbier and Álvaro Palacios settled around the village of Gratallops. Their first wines, from the 1989 vintage, showed what the old vines and llicorella could do.
Priorat later became Spain's second DOCa, or DOQ in Catalan. It has since added a village tier, Vi de Vila.

Montsant almost surrounds Priorat. It was once a subzone of the Tarragona DO and became a DO in its own right in 2001. It uses the same main grapes, Garnacha and Cariñena, but has more varied soils with less llicorella. The wines are usually softer and better value.

Penedès lies south-west of Barcelona, between the coast and the inland hills. It rises from the warm Baix Penedès near the sea to the higher, cooler Alt Penedès. It makes still wines from local and international grapes, and it is the heart of Cava production.

Cava is a traditional method sparkling wine, with the second fermentation in the bottle. Unusually, the DO is not one continuous area. It is a list of municipalities in several parts of Spain, including Aragón, Navarra, La Rioja, the Basque Country, Valencia and Extremadura. Most Cava is made in Penedès, around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia.
The traditional grapes are Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are also allowed. Josep Raventós of Codorníu made the first Cava in 1872.
Cava must spend at least 9 months on its lees. Cava Reserva needs at least 18 months, Gran Reserva at least 30 months, and Cava de Paraje Calificado, from a single site, at least 36 months.

Further south the climate turns hot and dry. Jumilla, inland in Murcia and Albacete, is the home of Monastrell, the grape called Mourvèdre in France. It needs plenty of heat to ripen. Vines are often bush trained and grown on poor, limestone soils.

Monastrell gives deep-coloured reds with ripe black fruit, high alcohol and firm tannins. Neighbouring Yecla and Alicante also rely on it. Alicante makes a rare, long-aged style from very ripe Monastrell called Fondillón.

key: Llicorella is Priorat's dark, brittle slate. It gives deep roots and very low yields.
Priorat is based on Garnacha and Cariñena. Its modern revival began with the 1989 vintage around Gratallops.
Montsant surrounds Priorat and became a DO in 2001, after being a subzone of Tarragona.
Cava is made by the traditional method from Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. Most is made around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia in Penedès.
Cava lees ageing minimums: 9 months, Reserva 18, Gran Reserva 30, Paraje Calificado 36.
Monastrell (Mourvèdre) is the grape of Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante.

questions.q: What is llicorella?
questions.explain: Llicorella is the dark slate of Priorat. It splits into thin layers and holds little water.

questions.q: Which two grapes are the traditional base of Priorat?
questions.explain: Garnacha and Cariñena, often from old bush vines, are the traditional grapes of Priorat.

questions.q: Which monastery's monks first planted vines in Priorat?
questions.explain: Carthusian monks founded the monastery of Scala Dei in the 12th century and planted vines there.

questions.q: Before becoming a DO in 2001, Montsant was a subzone of which DO?
questions.explain: Montsant was part of the Tarragona DO before gaining its own DO in 2001.

questions.q: What is the minimum time on lees for a basic Cava?
questions.explain: All Cava must spend at least 9 months on its lees. 18 months is the minimum for Cava Reserva.

questions.q: What is the minimum lees ageing for Cava Gran Reserva?
questions.explain: Cava Gran Reserva needs at least 30 months. 36 months applies to Cava de Paraje Calificado.

questions.q: Which grapes are the traditional trio for Cava?
options: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier
questions.explain: Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada are the traditional Cava grapes. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are also allowed.

questions.q: Monastrell, the grape of Jumilla, is known in France as which variety?
questions.explain: Monastrell is the Spanish name for Mourvèdre.

questions.q: Which village was at the heart of Priorat's revival in the late 1980s?
questions.explain: René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios and others settled around Gratallops. Their first wines came from the 1989 vintage.

questions.q: Which tier sits at the top of Priorat's origin classification?
questions.explain: The pyramid rises from DOQ Priorat through Vi de Vila, Vi de Paratge and Vinya Classificada to Gran Vinya Classificada.

questions.q: What is the minimum lees ageing for Cava Reserva?
questions.explain: Cava Reserva needs at least 18 months on its lees. 9 months is the minimum for all Cava and 30 for Gran Reserva.

questions.q: Which is NOT a requirement for Cava de Guarda Superior?
questions.explain: Guarda Superior Cava can come from any part of the DO. It needs organic grapes from vines at least 10 years old and shows the vintage.

questions.q: Why do Priorat vines root deeply and give very low yields?
options: Heavy irrigation draws the roots down
The soils are fertile and alluvial
questions.explain: Llicorella is brittle slate that holds little water, so the roots must go deep and the vines give little fruit.

questions.q: In which two provinces does Jumilla lie?
questions.explain: Jumilla lies inland in Murcia and Albacete, in the hot, dry south-east where Monastrell thrives.

questions.q: Fondillón is a long-aged wine from which grape and DO?
questions.explain: Fondillón is made in Alicante from overripe Monastrell and must age at least 10 years in oak.

questions.q: Which Catalan DO is best known for Garnacha Blanca?
questions.explain: Terra Alta, inland in the south of Catalunya, is the classic source of Garnacha Blanca.

cards.b: Priorat's dark, brittle slate. It splits into thin layers, holds little water and forces roots deep.
Garnacha and Cariñena (Carignan), often from old bush vines.

cards.f: Which village was the centre of Priorat's revival?
cards.b: Gratallops, where a group including René Barbier and Álvaro Palacios settled in the late 1980s.
A Carthusian monastery founded in Priorat in the 12th century. Its monks planted vines there.
DOQ Priorat, Vi de Vila (village), Vi de Paratge, Vinya Classificada and Gran Vinya Classificada.
DO that almost surrounds Priorat. Once a subzone of Tarragona, it became a DO in 2001.

cards.f: How does Montsant differ from Priorat?
cards.b: Same main grapes, but more varied soils with less llicorella. The wines are usually softer.
DO south-west of Barcelona, rising from warm Baix Penedès near the sea to cooler, higher Alt Penedès.
The town in Penedès at the heart of Cava production.
Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are also allowed.

cards.f: Why is Cava unusual as a DO?
cards.b: It is not one continuous area but a list of municipalities in several parts of Spain.
The Cava zone covering the Cava areas of Catalunya, created in the 2021 zoning reform.
The basic Cava category, with at least 9 months on the lees.
Reserva (18 months), Gran Reserva (30) and Paraje Calificado (36). Organic grapes from vines at least 10 years old.
A Cava from a single qualified site, with at least 36 months on the lees.

cards.f: Who made the first Cava, and when?
cards.b: Josep Raventós of Codorníu, in 1872.
Spain's name for Mourvèdre. It needs plenty of heat and gives deep, tannic, high-alcohol reds.
Inland in the hot, dry south-east, across the provinces of Murcia and Albacete.
A rare Alicante wine from overripe Monastrell, aged at least 10 years in oak, with at least 16% natural alcohol.
A Catalan DO in the south-west of Tarragona province, known for Garnacha Blanca.

lessons.title: Jerez and sherry
lessons.intro: This lesson explains where sherry comes from, why albariza and Palomino matter, how flor and the solera work, and how the main styles from fino to Pedro Ximénez differ.

p: Sherry comes mainly from the province of Cádiz in Andalucía, in the far south-west of Spain. The DO is Jerez-Xérès-Sherry, its name in Spanish, French and English. Traditionally the wine is aged in three towns that form the sherry triangle: Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Since 2022 it may also be aged in the other towns of the production zone, but under the current rules fino may no longer be aged in Sanlúcar, the home of manzanilla.
The climate is hot and sunny. Two winds matter. The poniente blows in from the Atlantic and brings humidity. The levante blows from the east and is hot and dry.

The best vineyards are on albariza, a bright white soil rich in calcium carbonate. It soaks up winter rain and holds it like a sponge. In summer its surface hardens into a crust that slows evaporation, so the vines get through the long dry season.

Palomino is the main grape. It gives a neutral, low-acid base wine that suits the sherry process. Pedro Ximénez (PX) and Moscatel are used for sweet wines. For PX the grapes are often laid out in the sun to dry and concentrate their sugar, a practice called asoleo.

The base wine is fermented dry and then classified. Wines chosen for fino and manzanilla are usually fortified to about 15 to 15.5% abv. Since 2025 fortification is optional, and the legal minimum for both is now 14%. In butts that are not filled to the top, a film of yeast called flor grows on the surface. Flor shields the wine from oxygen and feeds on alcohol and glycerol. This is called biological ageing.

Flor gives a pale wine with sharp, pungent aromas of bread dough and almond. Wines chosen for oloroso are usually fortified to about 17% or more. At this strength flor cannot survive, so the wine ages in contact with oxygen. This oxidative ageing darkens the colour and gives nutty, toasty, dried fruit flavours.

Sherry is aged in a solera system. Butts are grouped in tiers by age. The oldest tier is itself called the solera, and the younger tiers are the criaderas. Wine for bottling is drawn from the solera, which is then topped up from the next oldest criadera, and so on up the line.

Because younger wine is constantly blended into older wine, the style stays consistent and most sherry carries no vintage. In biological soleras, the fresh wine also feeds the flor. VOS (Very Old Sherry) and VORS (Very Old Rare Sherry) are certified as at least 20 and 30 years old on average.

Fino is pale, dry and tangy, aged entirely under flor. Manzanilla is the same style aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, with its own DO, Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda. The cool, humid sea air keeps the flor thick, and the wine is light and salty. Both are best drunk fresh and chilled.

Amontillado starts under flor. When the flor fades, it is usually fortified further and ages on in contact with oxygen, becoming amber, dry and nutty. Oloroso is aged only oxidatively: dark, rich and naturally dry. Pedro Ximénez is intensely sweet, dark and raisined. Cream sherry is a sweetened blend, often of oloroso and PX.
Nearby Montilla-Moriles, in the province of Córdoba, makes similar styles mainly from Pedro Ximénez. Its finos often reach their strength naturally, without fortification.

key: Sherry is traditionally aged in Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda.
Albariza is a white soil rich in calcium carbonate that stores winter rain.
Palomino makes the dry styles. PX and Moscatel make the sweet ones, PX often from sun-dried grapes.
Fino and manzanilla are usually fortified to about 15 to 15.5% (fortification is now optional) and age under flor. Oloroso is usually fortified to about 17% or more and ages oxidatively.
In a solera, wine is drawn from the oldest tier and topped up from the criaderas, so most sherry has no vintage.
Manzanilla must be aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Amontillado starts under flor and finishes oxidatively.

questions.q: In which town must manzanilla be aged?
questions.explain: Manzanilla is fino-style sherry aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, with its own DO, Manzanilla-Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

questions.q: What is albariza?
options: A white soil rich in calcium carbonate
questions.explain: Albariza is the bright white soil of Jerez. It stores winter rain and forms a crust in summer.

questions.q: Which grape is the main variety for dry sherry?
questions.explain: Palomino gives the neutral, low-acid base wine used for the dry styles. PX and Moscatel are used for sweet wines.

questions.q: What does flor do to a fino as it ages?
options: It adds sugar to the wine
It shields the wine from oxygen
questions.explain: Flor forms a film on the wine that protects it from oxygen, while it feeds on alcohol and glycerol.

questions.q: To roughly what strength is a wine fortified when it is chosen for oloroso?
questions.explain: Oloroso is fortified to about 17% or more, which prevents flor from growing, so the wine ages oxidatively.

questions.q: In a solera system, what is the oldest tier of butts called?
questions.explain: The oldest tier is the solera. Wine is drawn from it and topped up from the younger criaderas.

questions.q: How is amontillado made?
options: It is aged oxidatively from the start
It is a sweetened blend of oloroso and PX
It is aged entirely under flor
It starts under flor, then ages in contact with oxygen
questions.explain: Amontillado begins as a fino under flor. When the flor fades it continues ageing oxidatively, becoming amber and nutty.

questions.q: What is asoleo?
options: Drying grapes in the sun to concentrate sugar
Adding grape spirit to the base wine
Drawing wine from the oldest tier
questions.explain: Asoleo is the practice of laying grapes, usually Pedro Ximénez, in the sun to dry before pressing.

questions.q: Which wind brings humidity to Jerez from the Atlantic?
questions.explain: The poniente blows in from the Atlantic and brings humidity. The levante is hot and dry, from the east.

questions.q: What is the minimum sugar content of a Pedro Ximénez sherry?
questions.explain: PX must have at least 212 g/l of sugar. 160 g/l is the minimum for Moscatel and 115 g/l the floor for Cream.

questions.q: What minimum average age does VORS on a sherry label certify?
questions.explain: VORS, Very Old Rare Sherry, certifies an average age of over 30 years. VOS certifies over 20.

questions.q: Which style combines the aroma of an amontillado with the body of an oloroso?
questions.explain: Palo cortado is a dry generoso that sits between amontillado and oloroso in style.

questions.q: Why does flor stay thick in Sanlúcar de Barrameda?
questions.explain: Sanlúcar sits at the mouth of the Guadalquivir. Its cool, humid sea air keeps the flor thick, giving light, salty manzanilla.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a dry generoso style?
questions.explain: Cream is a sweetened vino generoso de licor. Fino, amontillado and oloroso have at most 4 g/l of sugar.

questions.q: What does en rama mean on a sherry label?
questions.explain: En rama sherry is bottled with minimal treatment: the only stabilisation allowed is filtration.

questions.q: Which DO in the province of Córdoba makes sherry-like wines mainly from Pedro Ximénez?
questions.explain: Montilla-Moriles is in Córdoba. Its warm climate lets Pedro Ximénez reach high natural strength.

cards.b: The sherry DO, named in Spanish, French and English. Its vineyards are in the province of Cádiz.
Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar de Barrameda.

cards.f: Can sherry be aged outside the triangle today?
cards.b: Yes. Since 2022 ageing may also take place in the other municipalities of the production zone.
The poniente is a humid wind from the Atlantic. The levante is a hot, dry wind from the east.
Bright white soil rich in calcium carbonate. It stores winter rain and forms a summer crust that slows evaporation.
The main grape for dry sherry. It gives a neutral, low-acid base wine.
Laying grapes in the sun to dry and concentrate their sugar, above all for Pedro Ximénez.
A film of yeast on wine in part-filled butts. It shields the wine from oxygen and feeds on alcohol and glycerol.
The solera is the oldest tier of butts. The criaderas are the younger tiers that top it up.
Two years under the DO rules.

cards.f: Maximum butt size for sherry ageing
cards.b: 1,000 litres, though larger historic vessels can be recognized by the Consejo Regulador.
Certified average ages of over 20 years (VOS) and over 30 years (VORS). 12 and 15 year statements also exist.
Biologically aged wines with an average age of at least seven years.
Fino-style sherry aged in Sanlúcar de Barrameda, under its own DO. Sea air keeps the flor thick.
A dry generoso with the delicate aroma of an amontillado and the body of an oloroso.
Fino, amontillado, palo cortado and oloroso have at most 4 g/l of sugar.
Intensely sweet, dark and raisined, with at least 212 g/l of sugar.
A sweetened blend, often oloroso with PX, with 115 to 140 g/l of sugar.
A sherry bottled with no stabilisation other than filtration.
DO in Córdoba making sherry-like wines mainly from Pedro Ximénez. Its finos often need no fortification.

lessons.title: Portugal
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the Douro and the main styles of Port, the table wine regions of Vinho Verde, Dão and Alentejo, and a brief look at Madeira.

p: The Douro river runs west across northern Portugal from Spain to the sea at Porto. In 1756, under the Marquês de Pombal, the Douro became one of the first demarcated wine regions in the world. Vines grow on steep slopes of schist, often on terraces. Mountains to the west block much of the Atlantic rain, so summers are hot and dry.

There are three subregions. Baixo Corgo, in the west, is the coolest and wettest. Cima Corgo, around Pinhão, is the heart of fine Port. Douro Superior, towards the Spanish border, is the hottest and driest. The region makes both Port, under the DO Porto, and unfortified wines, under the DO Douro.
Many grapes are allowed. The best known are Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão. They give deep colour, tannin and intense fruit.

Port is fortified during fermentation. Grape spirit (aguardente) at about 77% abv is added while the wine still holds much of its sugar. This stops fermentation and leaves a sweet wine of about 19 to 22% abv. Because fermentation is short, colour and tannin must be extracted fast, traditionally by treading in shallow stone troughs called lagares.
Port has traditionally been aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from the city of Porto.

Ruby styles age in large vessels to keep their fruit and colour. Reserve Ruby is a higher quality ruby. Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) comes from a single year and is bottled four to six years after harvest. Vintage Port is made only in declared years, bottled in its second or third year, and needs long ageing in bottle. It throws a sediment and needs decanting.

Tawny styles age in small casks, where slow oxidation turns them amber and gives nutty, dried fruit flavours. Tawnies with an indication of age, such as 10, 20, 30 or 40 years, show the average character of a blend. Colheita is a tawny from a single harvest, aged at least seven years in wood. White and rosé Port are also made.

Vinho Verde, in the rainy, green north-west, makes light, fresh whites, often low in alcohol and sometimes slightly sparkling. Verde means young, not green in colour. Key grapes are Alvarinho, Loureiro, Arinto and Avesso. In the subregion of Monção e Melgaço, on the Minho river facing Galicia, Alvarinho gives fuller wines. Red Vinho Verde is made mainly from Vinhão.

Dão lies on a granite plateau in central Portugal, ringed by mountains such as the Serra da Estrela, which shelter it from Atlantic rain and continental extremes. Reds from Touriga Nacional, Jaen (Mencía) and Alfrocheiro are fresh and elegant. Encruzado is the leading white grape.

Alentejo, in the south, is hot, dry and mostly flat, with forests of cork oak. Reds come from Aragonez (Tempranillo), Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet. Antão Vaz and Arinto are key whites. The old practice of fermenting in large clay jars survives in the DO's Vinho de Talha wines.

Madeira is an island in the Atlantic, west of Morocco. Its fortified wine is heated during ageing, a practice that grew from the discovery that the wine improved on long tropical sea voyages. In estufagem the wine is heated in tanks for at least three months. The finest wines use the canteiro method, ageing slowly in casks in warm lofts.

Four classic grapes also name the sweetness. Sercial is the driest, then Verdelho, Boal (Bual) and Malvasia (Malmsey), the sweetest. Tinta Negra is the most planted grape. All styles keep high acidity, and because they are already heated and oxidised they last for decades, even once opened. Unfortified wines from the island use the DO Madeirense.

key: The Douro was demarcated in 1756 under the Marquês de Pombal. Its vineyards are on steep schist slopes.
Douro subregions from west to east: Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior, getting hotter and drier.
Port is fortified with grape spirit during fermentation, which leaves natural sweetness.
LBV is bottled four to six years after harvest. Vintage Port is bottled in its second or third year. Colheita is a single-harvest tawny with at least seven years in wood.
Vinho Verde is fresh and light. Alvarinho is the grape of Monção e Melgaço. Dão is a granite plateau with Touriga Nacional and Encruzado.
Madeira is heated during ageing. Sercial is the driest style and Malvasia (Malmsey) the sweetest.

questions.q: In which year was the Douro demarcated under the Marquês de Pombal?
questions.explain: The Douro was demarcated in 1756, making it one of the first demarcated wine regions in the world.

questions.q: What is the main soil of the Douro vineyards?
questions.explain: Douro vines grow on steep slopes of schist, often on terraces.

questions.q: Which Douro subregion, towards the Spanish border, is the hottest and driest?
questions.explain: Douro Superior in the east is the hottest and driest. Baixo Corgo in the west is the coolest and wettest.

questions.q: Why is Port sweet?
options: Grape spirit is added during fermentation, stopping it before all the sugar is used
The grapes are dried in the sun before pressing
A sweetened wine is blended in before bottling
questions.explain: Adding aguardente at about 77% abv stops fermentation and leaves some of the grape sugar in the wine.

questions.q: When is a Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) Port bottled?
options: In its second or third year
Four to six years after harvest
After at least seven years in wood
After at least ten years in wood
questions.explain: LBV is bottled four to six years after harvest. Vintage Port is bottled in its second or third year.

questions.q: What is a Colheita Port?
options: A ruby blend from several years
A white Port aged in large vats
A tawny from a single harvest aged at least seven years in wood
A Vintage Port from a single estate
questions.explain: Colheita is a single-harvest tawny that must spend at least seven years in wood.

questions.q: In which Vinho Verde subregion does Alvarinho give its fullest wines?
questions.explain: Monção e Melgaço, on the Minho river facing Galicia, is the home of fuller Alvarinho.

questions.q: Which is the driest of the classic Madeira styles?
questions.explain: Sercial is the driest, followed by Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia (Malmsey), the sweetest.

questions.q: What strength of grape spirit is used to fortify Port?
questions.explain: Port is fortified with aguardente at about 77% abv, which stops fermentation and leaves a wine of about 19 to 22%.

questions.q: What is a Crusted Port?
options: A blend of years kept at least three years in bottle before sale
A white Port aged in cask
A Vintage Port from one quinta
questions.explain: Crusted Port is a blend of years that ages in bottle, where it throws a crust of sediment. A single-harvest tawny is a Colheita.

questions.q: Until 1986, from where did all Port for export have to be shipped?
options: The Vila Nova de Gaia entrepôt
questions.explain: All export Port had to leave from the Gaia entrepôt. Since 1986 it can be shipped from anywhere in the Douro demarcation.

questions.q: Which Madeira category must spend at least 20 years in cask?
questions.explain: Frasqueira is a single-vintage Madeira with at least 20 years in wood. A Madeira Colheita needs at least five.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an age indication used for tawny Port?
questions.explain: Tawnies with an indication of age are labelled 10, 20, 30, 40 or, since 2022, 50 years. There is no 25-year category.

questions.q: Which grape is the leading white of Dão?
questions.explain: Encruzado is Dão's key white. Alvarinho and Loureiro belong to Vinho Verde, and Antão Vaz to Alentejo.

questions.q: Why must colour and tannin be extracted fast when making Port?
options: The must is heated in estufas
The wine goes straight into bottle
questions.explain: Grape spirit is added part way through fermentation, so there is little time on the skins. Treading in lagares speeds up extraction.

questions.q: In which region does fermenting in large clay jars survive as Vinho de Talha?
questions.explain: Vinho de Talha is an Alentejo wine made in clay jars, an old practice kept alive within the DO.

cards.b: In 1756, under the Marquês de Pombal, one of the first demarcated wine regions in the world.
Schist on steep slopes, often terraced.
Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo and Douro Superior. They get hotter and drier towards the east.
Town at the heart of Cima Corgo, the core of fine Port production.
Port is made under DO Porto. Unfortified wines from the same region use DO Douro.
Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão.
Grape spirit of about 77% abv, added during fermentation to make Port.
A shallow stone trough where grapes are trodden to extract colour and tannin quickly.
Town across the Douro from Porto, where Port has traditionally aged in the shippers' lodges.

cards.f: What changed for Port exports in 1986?
cards.b: Port no longer had to be shipped from the Gaia entrepôt, so Douro estates could export directly.
A single-year ruby, bottled after four to six years in wood.
A blend of years, kept at least three years in bottle before sale. It throws a sediment.
From a single declared year, bottled two to three years after harvest. It needs long bottle age and decanting.
A tawny from a single harvest, aged at least seven years in wood.
Nine: Monção e Melgaço, Lima, Cávado, Ave, Basto, Sousa, Amarante, Baião and Paiva.
Granite plateau ringed by mountains such as the Serra da Estrela. Touriga Nacional and Encruzado lead.
Alentejo wine fermented in large clay jars, an old practice kept alive within the DO.
Estufagem heats Madeira in tanks for at least three months. Canteiro ages it slowly in casks in warm lofts.

cards.f: Madeira styles from driest to sweetest
cards.b: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal (Bual), Malvasia (Malmsey).
Both from a single vintage. Frasqueira needs at least 20 years in cask, Colheita at least five years.

paths.title: Germany and Austria
paths.summary: How German and Austrian wine law works and how to read the labels, then the key regions: the Mosel, the Rhine regions, Germany's red wine and outer regions, and Austria from the Wachau to the Neusiedlersee.

lessons.title: German wine law and labels
lessons.intro: German labels carry a lot of information once you know the code. This lesson covers the quality categories, the six Prädikat levels, the sweetness terms, the place hierarchy of the 1971 wine law and the VDP's private classification, which sits outside the law.

p: German wine law sorts wine into four tiers. Deutscher Wein (once called Tafelwein) and Landwein are the basic levels, Landwein being Germany's protected geographical indication. Above them come the two protected designations of origin: Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein.

Qualitätswein must come from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete, the official wine-growing regions, and the label must name that region. The must may be enriched with sugar before fermentation (chaptalisation). Every Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein passes an official analysis and tasting and carries an AP number, the Amtliche Prüfungsnummer.
Prädikatswein was called Qualitätswein mit Prädikat (QmP) until 2007. It must reach a set ripeness at harvest and may not be enriched. Its sugar and alcohol come from the grapes alone.

The six Prädikate are set by must weight, the sugar content of the grape juice at harvest. In rising order: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, with Eiswein sharing the Beerenauslese minimum. The level tells you how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the finished wine is.

Kabinett is the lightest. Spätlese means late harvest. Auslese is made from selected bunches. Beerenauslese (BA) uses individually selected overripe berries, usually affected by noble rot. Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) uses shrivelled, botrytised berries and gives very sweet, concentrated wine. Eiswein is pressed from grapes frozen on the vine and must reach the same minimum must weight as a Beerenauslese.

Because a Prädikat measures ripeness, a Spätlese or Auslese can be fermented dry. The label then adds a sweetness term. Trocken means dry and halbtrocken means off-dry; both are defined in law. Lieblich and süß describe clearly sweet wines.

Feinherb is widely used for off-dry wines but has no legal definition, so its meaning varies by producer. A Kabinett or Spätlese with no sweetness term on the label is often made in a fruity style with residual sugar, especially in the Mosel, but you cannot assume it.

The 1971 wine law divides each Anbaugebiet into Bereiche (districts), Großlagen (collective sites) and Einzellagen (single vineyards). Place names are usually written as the village plus the suffix -er, then the site: Wehlener Sonnenuhr means the Sonnenuhr vineyard of Wehlen.

A Großlage groups many single vineyards, sometimes across several villages, and is named in exactly the same village plus site style. Piesporter Michelsberg is a large Großlage, while Piesporter Goldtröpfchen is a famous Einzellage. Niersteiner Gutes Domtal in Rheinhessen is another Großlage known for simple bulk wine. Under the 1971 rules nothing on the label told the drinker which kind of site was meant. From the 2026 vintage, a Großlage or Bereich name on the label must be preceded by the word Region.

The VDP (Verband Deutscher Prädikatsweingüter) is an association of leading estates whose roots go back to 1910. Members put an eagle with a grape cluster on the capsule. Its classification is private: it binds only members and is not part of German wine law.

The VDP pyramid has four levels: VDP.Gutswein, VDP.Ortswein, VDP.Erste Lage and VDP.Große Lage. A dry wine from a Große Lage is called Großes Gewächs (GG). VDP members generally keep Prädikat names for wines with natural residual sugar. Do not confuse the VDP's Große Lage, its top sites, with the legal Großlage, a collective site.
In 2021 the wine law itself was amended to give origin more weight, a change that is being phased in.

key: Germany has 13 Anbaugebiete for Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein.
Prädikatswein may not be chaptalised; Qualitätswein may.
The Prädikate, in rising order of must weight: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese; Eiswein has the same minimum as Beerenauslese.
Trocken and halbtrocken are legally defined; feinherb is not.
A Großlage is a collective site under the 1971 law; until the 2026 vintage it was labelled like a single vineyard.
The VDP classification (Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage, Große Lage) is private; Großes Gewächs is a dry wine from a Große Lage.

questions.q: How many Anbaugebiete can produce German Qualitätswein?
questions.explain: German Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein must come from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete, the official quality wine regions.

questions.q: Which German category may not be enriched with sugar before fermentation?
questions.explain: Prädikatswein must reach its ripeness naturally and may not be chaptalised. Qualitätswein may be enriched.

questions.q: What do the German Prädikat levels measure?
options: Residual sugar in the finished wine
Must weight of the grapes at harvest
questions.explain: Prädikate are based on the sugar content of the must at harvest, so a Spätlese can still be fermented fully dry.

questions.q: Which Prädikat is pressed from grapes frozen on the vine?
questions.explain: Eiswein is made from grapes frozen on the vine and must reach the same minimum must weight as a Beerenauslese.

questions.q: What does feinherb on a German label mean?
options: A legally defined term for bone-dry wine
An unregulated term usually used for off-dry wine
A Prädikat level between Kabinett and Spätlese
The VDP name for its top vineyards
questions.explain: Feinherb is widely used for off-dry wines but has no legal definition, unlike trocken and halbtrocken.

questions.q: Under the 1971 wine law, what is Piesporter Michelsberg?
questions.explain: Michelsberg is a Großlage, a collective site that groups many vineyards. Piesporter Goldtröpfchen is the famous single vineyard.

questions.q: What is a Großes Gewächs (GG)?
options: A dry wine from a VDP Große Lage
A sweet wine from a legal Großlage
questions.explain: In the VDP's private classification, GG is the name for a dry wine from one of its top sites, a Große Lage.

questions.q: Which statement about the VDP classification is correct?
options: It was set out in the 1971 wine law
It was introduced by the EU in 2009
It applies to every producer in a region
It is a private classification that binds only member estates
questions.explain: The VDP is an association of estates. Its four-level classification is private and separate from German wine law.

questions.q: What is the minimum actual alcohol for a German Beerenauslese?
questions.explain: German law sets 5.5% abv for Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein. Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese need 7%.

questions.q: Without the acidity allowance, up to how much sugar may a wine be labelled trocken?
questions.explain: Trocken allows up to 4 g/l, or up to 9 g/l if acidity is close enough to the sugar. 12 g/l is the basic halbtrocken limit.

questions.q: What was Prädikatswein called before 2007?
questions.explain: The category was renamed from Qualitätswein mit Prädikat to Prädikatswein in 2007.

questions.q: Which is the top level of Germany's legal origin pyramid from the 2026 vintage?
questions.explain: The pyramid narrows from Gebietswein (whole region) through Regionenwein and Ortswein (village) to Lagenwein (single vineyard).

questions.q: How many Landwein areas does Germany have?
questions.explain: Germany has 26 Landwein areas for its PGI wines. 13 is the number of Anbaugebiete for Qualitätswein.

questions.q: Which term on a German label has NO legal definition?
questions.explain: Trocken, halbtrocken and lieblich are defined by sugar limits. Feinherb is unregulated, so its meaning varies by producer.

questions.q: What does the AP number on a German label show?
options: That the wine passed official analysis and tasting
questions.explain: Every Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein must pass an official test and receives an Amtliche Prüfungsnummer.

questions.q: In the name Wehlener Sonnenuhr, what does Wehlener refer to?
questions.explain: German site names put the village first with the suffix -er, then the vineyard. Sonnenuhr is the vineyard.

cards.b: One of Germany's 13 official wine regions for Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein.
Germany's PGI tier. There are 26 Landwein areas.
Amtliche Prüfungsnummer: proof that a Qualitätswein or Prädikatswein passed official analysis and tasting.
Qualitätswein mit Prädikat (QmP).
No. Its sugar and alcohol must come from the grapes alone. Qualitätswein may be enriched.

cards.f: The Prädikate in rising order of must weight
cards.b: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese. Eiswein shares the Beerenauslese minimum.
The German scale of must weight, the sugar content of the grape juice at harvest.

cards.f: Minimum actual alcohol: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese
cards.b: 7% abv, the same as for Qualitätswein.

cards.f: Minimum actual alcohol: Beerenauslese, TBA, Eiswein

cards.b: Made from individually selected overripe berries, usually affected by noble rot.
Pressed from grapes frozen on the vine. It must reach at least the Beerenauslese must weight.
Dry: up to 4 g/l of sugar, or up to 9 g/l if total acidity is no more than 2 g/l below the sugar.
Off-dry: up to 12 g/l of sugar, or up to 18 g/l if total acidity is no more than 10 g/l below the sugar.
Lieblich wines have up to 45 g/l of sugar. Süß wines have at least 45 g/l.
Widely used for off-dry wine, but it has no legal definition.

cards.f: How do you read Wehlener Sonnenuhr?
cards.b: The village Wehlen plus -er, then the vineyard: the Sonnenuhr site of Wehlen.
A collective site under the 1971 law, grouping many vineyards. It was labelled exactly like a single vineyard.

cards.f: Germany's origin pyramid from the 2026 vintage

A private pyramid binding only members: VDP.Gutswein, VDP.Ortswein, VDP.Erste Lage, VDP.Große Lage.
A dry wine from a VDP Große Lage. Do not confuse Große Lage with the legal Großlage.

lessons.title: The Mosel
lessons.intro: The Mosel is the home of light, racy Riesling grown on slate. This lesson covers the river's landscape and soils, the Mosel style, the great villages of the Middle Mosel, the cooler Saar and Ruwer, and the Großlage names to watch for.

p: The Mosel rises in the Vosges in France, forms part of the border with Luxembourg and joins the Rhine at Koblenz. The region was called Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007, when it was renamed Mosel. It is cool and northerly, so site is everything.

The best vineyards sit on steep slopes above the river's tight meanders, facing south or south-west. Devonian slate dominates. The dark stone absorbs heat by day and the river reflects light onto the vines. Many slopes can only be worked by hand. The Calmont at Bremm is often called one of the steepest vineyards in Europe.

Riesling dominates the quality vineyards. Classic Mosel Riesling is light in body and alcohol, with high acidity and aromas of green apple, citrus and peach, often with a stony or smoky note. Many Kabinett and Spätlese wines keep residual sugar that balances the acidity, though dry wines are now common too.
The Upper Mosel (Obermosel), near Luxembourg, lies on limestone rather than slate. Here the old Elbling grape is still grown, often for sparkling wine.

The Middle Mosel (Mittelmosel) is the heart of the region. Bernkastel is known for the Doctor vineyard, among the most famous in Germany. Wehlen's Sonnenuhr takes its name from a sundial in the vineyard. Graach, Zeltingen, Ürzig, with its red soils in the Würzgarten, and Brauneberg are other great names.

Upriver, Piesport's Goldtröpfchen is a south-facing slope shaped like an amphitheatre. These villages also give their names to Großlagen: Bernkasteler Badstube and Kurfürstlay, Graacher Münzlay for Wehlen, Graach and Zeltingen, and Piesporter Michelsberg.

The Saar and the Ruwer are tributaries that join the Mosel near Trier. Both valleys are cooler than the Middle Mosel. In cool years the grapes struggle to ripen; in warm years the wines are some of the most finely etched Rieslings in the world, with steely acidity.

The Scharzhofberg at Wiltingen is the Saar's most famous vineyard; the whole Saar falls in the Großlage Scharzberg. On the Ruwer, Maximin Grünhaus and the Karthäuserhofberg at Eitelsbach are the best-known estates and sites. Trier and the Ruwer share the Großlage Römerlay.
Downstream towards Koblenz, the Lower Mosel is also called the Terrassenmosel for its terraced slopes. The Calmont lies here.

Some Mosel Großlagen are better known than any vineyard in them because they were used for large volumes of simple wine. Zeller Schwarze Katz, with its black cat label, and Kröver Nacktarsch are the classic examples. They show why reading the site name alone can mislead.

key: The region was named Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007.
Steep south-facing slopes of Devonian slate above the river give the best sites.
Classic Mosel Riesling: low alcohol, high acidity, often balanced by residual sugar.
Great Middle Mosel sites: Bernkasteler Doctor, Wehlener Sonnenuhr, Piesporter Goldtröpfchen.
The Saar and Ruwer are cooler side valleys; Scharzhofberg is the Saar's top vineyard.
The Upper Mosel lies on limestone and grows Elbling.

questions.q: What was the Mosel region called until 2007?
questions.explain: The Anbaugebiet was renamed from Mosel-Saar-Ruwer to Mosel in 2007.

questions.explain: The Wehlener Sonnenuhr is named after the sundial set in the vineyard.

A south-facing slope shaped like an amphitheatre

options: They are warmer and give fuller wines
They are cooler, with harder ripening in cool years and steely acidity
They are planted mainly to red grapes
They lie on limestone rather than slate
questions.explain: Both side valleys are cooler. In good years they give very fine Riesling with steely acidity.

questions.explain: The Upper Mosel near Luxembourg lies on limestone, and the old Elbling grape survives there.

questions.q: Zeller Schwarze Katz and Kröver Nacktarsch are examples of what?
options: Großlagen widely used for simple wine
questions.explain: Both are Großlagen whose names became famous through large volumes of simple wine.

options: Full body, high alcohol, low acidity
Light body, low alcohol, high acidity, often with some residual sugar
questions.explain: Mosel Kabinett is light and racy, and residual sugar often balances its high acidity.

questions.q: Where does the Mosel join the Rhine?
questions.explain: The Mosel flows into the Rhine at Koblenz. The Nahe joins the Rhine at Bingen.

questions.explain: Both tributaries reach the Mosel near Trier, upstream of the Middle Mosel.

questions.explain: Mittelhaardt is the Riesling heart of the Pfalz. Bernkastel, Burg Cochem and Obermosel are all Mosel Bereiche.

questions.q: How does slate help the vines ripen on the Mosel?
options: The dark stone absorbs heat by day
It holds a lot of water
questions.explain: Dark slate warms in the sun and gives off heat, which helps grapes ripen at this northern latitude.

questions.q: Where is the Calmont vineyard?
options: At Bremm in the Lower Mosel
At Piesport in the Middle Mosel
questions.explain: The Calmont rises above the river at Bremm in the Lower Mosel, the Terrassenmosel.

questions.q: Which Großlage covers the whole Saar?
questions.explain: The whole Saar falls in the Großlage Scharzberg. Römerlay covers Trier and the Ruwer.

Terraced vineyard at Bremm in the Lower Mosel, often called one of the steepest in Europe.

One of Germany's most famous vineyards, above Bernkastel in the Middle Mosel.

lessons.title: The Rhine regions
lessons.intro: This lesson covers five Anbaugebiete on the Rhine and its tributary the Nahe. It covers the Rheingau, Rheinhessen and its Roter Hang, the Pfalz, the Nahe and the Mittelrhein gorge.

p: Between Wiesbaden and Rüdesheim the Rhine flows from east to west, so the vineyards on its north bank face south. The Taunus hills shelter them from cold north winds. Riesling is the main grape, with Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) second, famously at Assmannshausen on the bend of the river.

The Rheingau has a long history. Tradition says the value of late-harvested grapes was discovered at Schloss Johannisberg in 1775, when the courier bringing permission to pick arrived late. The Cistercians of Kloster Eberbach shaped its vineyards. Hochheim, on the Main, gave the English word hock for Rhine wine.

Rheinhessen is Germany's largest Anbaugebiet by vineyard area, a gentle landscape of rolling hills inside the bend of the Rhine. It was long known for bulk wine such as Liebfraumilch and for Müller-Thurgau and Silvaner. Since the 1990s, a new generation of growers has transformed its reputation.

The Rheinterrasse is a band of slopes along the river at Nackenheim, Nierstein and Oppenheim. Its heart is the Roter Hang, the red slope, where red Permian clay-slate and sandstone give rich, spicy Riesling. Pettenthal and Hipping, two Roter Hang sites, lie in the Großlage Rehbach. In the south, the Wonnegau around Westhofen has become a source of top dry Riesling from limestone.

The Pfalz lies west of the Rhine and north of Alsace. The Haardt mountains, the northern continuation of the Vosges, put it in a rain shadow, so it is one of Germany's warmest and driest regions. Almonds and figs grow along the Deutsche Weinstraße, the wine road.

The Mittelhaardt, with Forst, Deidesheim, Wachenheim and Bad Dürkheim, is the Riesling heartland. Forst has patches of basalt, notably in the Pechstein vineyard. The Südliche Weinstraße to the south grows much Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder. The red crossing Dornfelder is also widely planted.

The Nahe flows from the west and joins the Rhine at Bingen. Its soils are unusually varied for a small region: volcanic rock, porphyry, slate, sandstone and quartzite all occur, sometimes within one village. The Rotenfels cliff near Bad Münster is a landmark.

Riesling is the leading grape. Nahe Riesling is often said to sit between the mineral delicacy of the Mosel and the weight of the Rheingau. Some of its finest sites lie in the middle Nahe: the Kupfergrube and Felsenberg at Schlossböckelheim and the Hermannshöhle at Niederhausen.

Below Bingen the Rhine cuts a narrow gorge through slate hills. This landscape of castles and terraces, including the Lorelei rock, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002 as the Upper Middle Rhine Valley.

The Mittelrhein is small. Its steep slate slopes grow mostly Riesling, with Bacharach and Boppard among the best-known villages. Steep slopes and hand work mean many vineyards have been abandoned over time.

key: In the Rheingau the Rhine flows east to west, so the main slopes face south; the Taunus shelters them.
Assmannshausen in the Rheingau is known for Spätburgunder.
Rheinhessen is Germany's largest Anbaugebiet; the Roter Hang at Nierstein has red Permian soils.
The Pfalz lies in the rain shadow of the Haardt, the continuation of the Vosges; the Mittelhaardt is its Riesling heart.
The Nahe is known for very varied soils, including volcanic rock and slate.
The Mittelrhein gorge is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with steep slate vineyards.

questions.q: What makes the Pfalz one of Germany's warmest and driest regions?
options: The rain shadow of the Haardt mountains

questions.explain: The Pechstein at Forst has basalt in its soil. The Saumagen at Kallstadt is a limestone site.

questions.q: What is southern Rheinhessen around Westhofen called?
questions.explain: The Wonnegau, around Westhofen, has become a source of top dry Riesling from limestone. The Rheinterrasse lies along the river at Nierstein.

questions.q: Monks of which abbey shaped the Rheingau's vineyards?
questions.explain: The Cistercians of Kloster Eberbach planted and walled the Steinberg. Scala Dei is in Priorat and Klosterneuburg in Austria.

Germany's largest Anbaugebiet by vineyard area, inside the bend of the Rhine.

lessons.title: Spätburgunder and Germany beyond the Rhine
lessons.intro: Germany is not only Riesling. This lesson covers the red wines of the Ahr and Baden, Silvaner in Franken, the red grapes of Württemberg, and the small northern regions of Saale-Unstrut and Sachsen.

sections.h: Ahr: red wine in the north
p: The Ahr is a narrow, steep valley that joins the Rhine south of Bonn. Although it is one of Germany's most northerly regions, it is planted mainly to red grapes. Slate and greywacke on steep slopes store heat and help ripening.

Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) is the main grape, joined by Frühburgunder, an early-ripening form of Pinot. The region has a single Großlage, Klosterberg. In July 2021 a severe flood caused great damage to the valley and its wineries.

Baden is Germany's most southerly region, stretching from the Tauberfranken in the north to Lake Constance (Bodensee). It is the only German region in EU wine-growing zone B, the same zone as Alsace, while the rest of Germany is in zone A.

The Burgunder family leads: Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder and Weißburgunder. The Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano covered in loess, is one of Germany's warmest spots. The Markgräflerland grows Gutedel (Chasselas), and the Ortenau, on granite, is known for Riesling, locally called Klingelberger.

Franken follows the river Main around Würzburg. The climate is continental, with cold winters and a risk of spring frost. Shell limestone (Muschelkalk) around Würzburg and Keuper further east are the main soils. The Würzburger Stein is the best-known vineyard.
Silvaner is the signature grape, giving dry, earthy, savoury wines; Müller-Thurgau is also widely planted. Franken wine is traditionally bottled in the Bocksbeutel, a flat, round flask.

Württemberg follows the Neckar and its tributaries around Stuttgart. It is unusual in Germany because red grapes dominate. Trollinger (the Schiava of Alto Adige) gives light, pale reds drunk locally. Lemberger (Blaufränkisch) gives deeper, firmer wines, and Schwarzriesling is Pinot Meunier.
Riesling is the main white grape. Cooperatives make a large share of the wine.

Saale-Unstrut and Sachsen lie in the former East Germany and are Germany's most north-easterly regions. Sachsen follows the Elbe around Dresden and Meissen. Both have a continental climate with frost risk, and both mostly make dry whites from grapes such as Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder and Riesling.
Hessische Bergstraße is a small region on the east side of the Rhine plain, south of Darmstadt, known mainly for Riesling.

Baden is Germany's only region in EU wine zone B; the Kaiserstuhl is an extinct volcano covered in loess.
Gutedel is Chasselas; Klingelberger is the Ortenau name for Riesling.
Franken: Silvaner on shell limestone, bottled in the Bocksbeutel.
Württemberg is red-dominated: Trollinger (Schiava), Lemberger (Blaufränkisch), Schwarzriesling (Pinot Meunier).
Sachsen lies on the Elbe around Dresden and Meissen.

The Baden name for Pinot Gris
