lessons.title: White and rosé winemaking
lessons.intro: This lesson follows white and rosé grapes from the press to the bottle: pressing and settling, cool fermentation, the choice of malolactic conversion, lees and bâtonnage, oak or steel, skin contact and orange wine, and the three ways to make rosé.

p: For white wine, speed and care matter, because the juice must stay fresh and free of bitter phenolics. Grapes may be crushed and destemmed, or pressed as whole bunches. Whole-bunch pressing is gentler and gives clearer juice with fewer phenolics, and Champagne and most fine sparkling wine use it.

Pneumatic presses squeeze the grapes slowly with an inflating membrane. The free-run juice, which flows before much pressure is applied, is the finest. Juice pressed out at higher pressure carries more phenolics and is kept apart or used for lesser wines.

Many winemakers protect the juice from oxygen with cold, sulphur dioxide and inert gas. This reductive handling keeps fresh fruit aromas, as in Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc. Others let the juice brown a little on purpose, so that the phenolics that would brown later drop out early.

Before fermentation the juice is clarified. In settling, or débourbage, it is chilled and left to stand, often overnight, so the solids sink and the clear juice can be drawn off. Some winemakers keep a little of the solids for texture and complexity.

Whites are usually fermented cool, at about 12 to 22°C, which keeps fruity and floral aromas. Stainless steel tanks with cooling jackets make this easy. Large old casks are traditional too: in the Mosel the Fuder holds about 1,000 litres and adds little oak flavour.
Fermentation can be stopped early to keep some sweetness, by chilling the wine, adding sulphur dioxide and filtering out the yeast. Many fruity Mosel Rieslings are made this way.

Malolactic conversion is carried out by lactic acid bacteria, mainly Oenococcus oeni, not by yeast. It turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, raises the pH slightly and can add the buttery aroma of diacetyl. It also makes the wine more stable, because the bacteria cannot start up later in the bottle.

For whites it is a style choice. Winemakers often allow it for full-bodied Chardonnay, as in Meursault, and block it for crisp, aromatic wines such as Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc. They block it with low temperature, sulphur dioxide and filtration, or let only part of the blend go through it.

After fermentation the dead yeast cells, the lees, settle out. Gross lees are coarse and usually removed. Fine lees can stay in contact with the wine for months, adding texture, a creamy or bready character and some protection from oxidation.

Muscadet sur lie stays on its fine lees through the winter and is bottled straight from them, which gives a fuller, slightly yeasty wine, sometimes with a faint prickle. In Bourgogne, Chardonnay fermented in barrel is often stirred, a practice called bâtonnage, to lift the lees back into the wine.

Oak changes a white in two ways. Fermenting in barrel integrates the oak and gives a creamy texture; ageing in barrel adds vanilla, toast and nutty notes and allows slow oxygen exchange. New barrels give the most flavour, older ones mainly texture. Many whites see no oak at all. Hunter Valley Semillon, picked early and made in steel, is light and lemony when young and turns toasty and honeyed after years in bottle.
A few hours of cold skin contact before pressing can draw more aroma from varieties such as Sauvignon Blanc or Muscat, at the risk of extra phenolics.

Orange or amber wine takes this much further. White grapes ferment and macerate on their skins for days, weeks or months, like a red. The wines are deeper in colour, with some tannin and flavours of dried fruit, nuts and tea. In Georgia, especially Kakheti, the method uses large clay jars called qvevri, buried in the ground; UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2013. Collio in Friuli and Goriška Brda across the border in Slovenia are modern centres of the style.

Rosé takes its colour from brief contact with the skins of black grapes. In direct pressing, the grapes are pressed at once and pick up only a faint colour. Many of the palest rosés of Côtes de Provence are made this way, often from Grenache, Cinsault and Syrah.

In short maceration, juice and skins stay together for a few hours to about two days before the juice is drawn off and fermented like a white. Tavel, a southern Rhône appellation for rosé only, makes deeper, fuller rosés this way. In saignée, some juice is bled from a tank of black grapes soon after crushing. It becomes rosé, and the red wine left behind is more concentrated.
In the EU, blending red and white wine to make rosé is generally not allowed. Rosé Champagne, which may blend in still red wine, is the classic exception.

key: Whole-bunch pressing is gentle and gives clear juice low in phenolics; free-run juice is the finest.
Débourbage settles the juice before a cool fermentation of about 12 to 22°C.
Malolactic conversion (Oenococcus oeni) softens acidity and can add buttery diacetyl. It is optional for whites.
Muscadet sur lie is bottled from its fine lees after one winter; bâtonnage stirs the lees in barrel.
Orange wine ferments white grapes on their skins; Georgia's qvevri method was listed by UNESCO in 2013.
Rosé: direct pressing (Côtes de Provence), short maceration (Tavel) or saignée.

questions.q: Why is whole-bunch pressing used for Champagne and fine sparkling wine?
options: It is gentle and gives clear juice low in phenolics
questions.explain: Pressing whole bunches gently limits phenolics and colour, which matters when black grapes are pressed for white sparkling wine.

questions.q: What is débourbage?
options: Removing the yeast after the second fermentation
Letting chilled juice settle so solids sink before fermentation
questions.explain: Settling clarifies the juice so that a clean fermentation follows.

questions.q: Which organism carries out most malolactic conversions?
questions.explain: Lactic acid bacteria, mainly Oenococcus oeni, turn malic acid into lactic acid. Saccharomyces is the wine yeast.

questions.q: How is Muscadet sur lie made?
options: It ages in new oak for two years
It is fermented on its skins
It is sweetened with grape must
It stays on its fine lees through the winter and is bottled from them
questions.explain: The wine is not racked off its fine lees before bottling, which adds texture and a yeasty note.

questions.q: In which country is wine fermented in buried clay jars called qvevri?
questions.explain: The qvevri method of Georgia, strong in Kakheti, was listed by UNESCO in 2013.

questions.q: Which southern Rhône appellation is for rosé only?
questions.explain: Tavel makes only rosé, deeper in colour than Provence rosé thanks to maceration.

questions.q: What is saignée?
options: Bleeding off some juice from a tank of black grapes
questions.explain: The bled juice becomes rosé and the red left in the tank is more concentrated.

questions.q: Which white wine is traditionally made without oak and ages for years to toasty, honeyed flavours?
questions.explain: Hunter Valley Semillon is picked early and made in steel, then develops toast and honey in bottle.

questions.q: What do juice fractions pressed at high pressure contain more of?
questions.explain: Harder pressing extracts more phenolics, so these fractions are kept apart or used in lesser wines.

questions.q: How long do juice and skins usually stay together for short-maceration rosé?
options: A few hours to about two days
questions.explain: After a few hours to about two days the juice is drawn off and fermented like a white.

questions.q: For which wine is malolactic conversion usually blocked?
questions.explain: Crisp, aromatic whites such as Riesling keep their malic acid. Full Bourgogne Chardonnay usually goes through it.

questions.q: What does bâtonnage add to a white wine?
questions.explain: Stirring the fine lees back into the wine gives more body and a creamy texture.

questions.q: About how much does a Mosel Fuder hold?
questions.explain: The Fuder holds about 1,000 litres; old Fuder add little oak flavour.

questions.q: Which region across the border from Collio is a modern centre of orange wine?
questions.explain: Goriška Brda in Slovenia faces Collio in Friuli; both are known for skin-fermented whites.

questions.q: Why are white wines usually fermented cool?
options: To keep fruity and floral aromas
questions.explain: Cool fermentation, about 12 to 22°C, keeps the delicate aromas that warmer fermentation would lose.

questions.q: Besides adding flavour, what does barrel ageing allow?
questions.explain: Oxygen passes slowly through the wood, which softens and develops the wine.

cards.b: Pressing uncrushed bunches. Gentle, with clear juice low in phenolics. Standard in Champagne.
Juice that flows before much pressure is applied. The finest and lowest in phenolics.
Juice bled from a tank of black grapes after brief contact. It makes rosé and concentrates the red left behind.
Protecting juice and wine from oxygen with cold, sulphur dioxide and inert gas to keep fresh fruit aromas.
Settling: chilled juice rests, often overnight, so solids sink and clear juice can be drawn off.
Usually about 12 to 22°C, cool enough to keep fruity and floral aromas.
The traditional Mosel cask of about 1,000 litres. Old Fuder add little oak flavour.

cards.f: How can fermentation be stopped to keep sweetness?
cards.b: By chilling, adding sulphur dioxide and filtering out the yeast.
Lactic acid bacteria turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, which can add buttery notes.
A by-product of malolactic conversion that smells of butter.
With low temperatures, sulphur dioxide and filtration that stop or remove the bacteria.
Gross lees are coarse solids removed early. Fine lees are small yeast particles that may stay to add texture.
Stays on its fine lees for one winter and is bottled from them, giving a fuller, slightly yeasty wine.
Stirring the lees in barrel or tank for body and a creamy texture. Common for Bourgogne Chardonnay.
Fermenting white juice in barrel. The oak integrates better and the texture is creamier than with ageing alone.
Picked early and made without oak: light and lemony young, toasty and honeyed after years in bottle.
White grapes fermented on their skins like a red, giving amber colour, tannin and dried fruit flavours.
Large Georgian clay jars buried in the ground for fermenting and ageing. UNESCO listed the method in 2013.
Black grapes pressed at once for very pale rosé. Typical of Côtes de Provence.
A southern Rhône appellation for rosé only. Maceration gives deeper, fuller wines.

lessons.title: Red winemaking and maturation
lessons.intro: This lesson covers how red wines gain colour, tannin and flavour, from crushing and cap management to whole bunches and carbonic maceration. It then follows the wine through maceration, pressing and oak, and on to fining, filtration and bottle ageing.

p: Black grapes are sorted, usually destemmed and lightly crushed so that juice and skins mix. The colour pigments, called anthocyanins, and much of the tannin sit in the skins. Seeds hold harsher tannin that is released if they are crushed or over-extracted.

Some winemakers keep the crushed grapes cool for a few days before fermentation, a cold soak or pre-fermentation maceration. It extracts colour and fruit into a water-based juice before alcohol forms, and it is popular for Pinot Noir in Bourgogne.

Red wine ferments warmer than white, at about 20 to 32°C, to help extraction. Carbon dioxide pushes the skins to the top, where they form a cap. The cap must be kept wet and mixed back into the juice, or it dries out and spoils, and extraction stops.

Pumping over (remontage) draws juice from the bottom of the tank and sprays it over the cap. Punching down (pigeage) pushes the cap into the juice by hand or by machine, and suits the small open vats often used for Pinot Noir. Rack and return (délestage) drains all the juice into another tank and pours it back over the cap, which also cools and aerates the ferment. Rotary fermenters turn the whole tank to mix skins and juice.

Some winemakers keep part or all of the bunches whole, stems included. Whole-bunch fermentation can add fresh, herbal and spicy notes, lift the aroma and soften the texture, but unripe stems add green tannin. It is used for some Pinot Noir in Bourgogne and Syrah in the northern Rhône.

In carbonic maceration, whole uncrushed bunches are put in a vessel filled with carbon dioxide. Without oxygen, an enzyme fermentation starts inside each berry and makes a little alcohol, about 2%, along with aromas of cherry, banana, bubblegum and kirsch. The berries then split, the grapes are pressed, and yeast finishes the fermentation.

Beaujolais uses semi-carbonic maceration. Bunches go whole into the vat; the lower ones are crushed by the weight above and ferment normally, while the upper ones go through carbonic maceration. The result is bright, fruity Gamay with low tannin. Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November. In crus such as Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, many producers macerate for longer to make firmer wines that age.

Maceration can be short or long. A few days give light, fruity reds. Two to four weeks, including time on the skins after fermentation, give deep-coloured, structured reds, and traditional Barolo producers have long used macerations of several weeks or more. A long maceration after fermentation is thought to make tannins feel softer, as they bind into longer chains.

The free-run wine is then drained off and the skins are pressed. Press wine is darker and more tannic. It is kept apart and blended back to taste. Almost all reds then go through malolactic conversion, in tank or in barrel.

Barrel size changes the effect. The smaller the barrel, the more wood each litre of wine touches. The Bordeaux barrique holds 225 litres and the Bourgogne pièce 228 litres. Large casks such as Italian botti or French foudres, often thousands of litres, add little oak flavour and allow slow, gentle contact with oxygen.

Age matters too. A new barrel gives the most vanilla, toast, spice and wood tannin. After several fills it gives little flavour but still lets in oxygen, which softens tannin and stabilises colour. Toasting the inside of the barrel over fire adds smoky, toasty notes.

Origin shapes flavour. French oak, from Quercus petraea and Quercus robur in forests such as Tronçais, Nevers and the Vosges, is tight-grained and gives subtle spice and toast. American oak, Quercus alba, gives stronger vanilla and coconut and was long the classic choice in Rioja. Slavonian oak from Croatia is traditional for large botti in Italy. Oak chips and staves are a cheaper way to add oak flavour.
Some reds must age by law. Barolo needs at least 38 months, 18 of them in wood, and Brunello di Montalcino at least two years in wood.

Before bottling, most wines are clarified and stabilised. Fining adds an agent that binds to unwanted particles and settles out. Egg white softens harsh tannin in red wine, bentonite clay removes proteins that could cloud a white, and gelatine, casein and PVPP are also used. In the EU, egg and milk products used for fining must be named on the label if they can be detected in the wine.

Filtration removes yeast, bacteria and haze. Coarse depth filters catch larger particles, while fine membrane filters can make a wine microbiologically stable. Cold stabilisation chills the wine so that tartrate crystals form in the tank instead of the bottle. Some producers prefer to bottle unfined and unfiltered and accept a deposit.

In bottle a fine red changes slowly. Tannins and colour pigments join together and some drop out as sediment, so the wine softens and the colour moves from purple to ruby, then garnet and brick. Fruit gives way to tertiary aromas such as leather, earth, forest floor and dried fruit. Wines with high acidity, tannin and concentration age longest, and old wines with a deposit need decanting.

key: Cap management: pumping over (remontage), punching down (pigeage), rack and return (délestage).
Carbonic maceration: whole bunches under carbon dioxide ferment inside the berry to about 2% alcohol. Beaujolais uses semi-carbonic.
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November.
Longer maceration gives deeper colour and more tannin; press wine is kept apart and blended back to taste.
Barrique 225 L (Bordeaux), pièce 228 L (Bourgogne); botti and foudres are large casks. French oak: Q. petraea and Q. robur; American oak: Q. alba.
Fining: egg white for reds, bentonite for whites. In bottle the colour moves from purple to brick and tertiary aromas develop.

questions.q: What is délestage?
options: Draining all the juice into another tank and pouring it back over the cap
Spraying juice over the cap with a pump
Keeping crushed grapes cold before fermentation
questions.explain: Délestage, rack and return, is vigorous and also cools and aerates the ferment. Pigeage is punching down and remontage is pumping over.

questions.q: About how much alcohol forms inside the berries during carbonic maceration?
questions.explain: The enzyme fermentation inside the berry makes about 2% alcohol before the grapes are pressed and yeast takes over.

questions.q: When is Beaujolais Nouveau released?
questions.explain: Beaujolais Nouveau goes on sale on the third Thursday of November of the harvest year.

questions.q: How large is a Bordeaux barrique?
questions.explain: The barrique holds 225 litres; the Bourgogne pièce holds 228.

questions.q: Which oak species is American oak?
questions.explain: American oak is Quercus alba. French oak comes from Q. robur and Q. petraea. Q. suber is the cork oak.

questions.q: Which fining agent removes proteins that could cloud a white wine?
questions.explain: Bentonite is a clay that binds proteins. Egg white is used mainly to soften tannin in reds.

questions.q: What is the purpose of cold stabilisation?
options: To make tartrate crystals form in the tank instead of the bottle
To kill wild yeast on the grapes
questions.explain: Chilling makes tartrates crystallise before bottling, so they do not appear in the bottle.

questions.q: How does the colour of a red wine change with age in bottle?
options: From purple through ruby and garnet to brick
questions.explain: As pigments and tannins bind and drop out, red wine loses its purple and moves towards garnet and brick.

questions.q: How large is the Bourgogne pièce?
questions.explain: The Bourgogne pièce holds 228 litres, slightly more than the 225 litre Bordeaux barrique.

questions.q: Why do winemakers avoid crushing grape seeds?
questions.explain: Crushed or over-extracted seeds give harsh, bitter tannin.

questions.q: What can a fine membrane filter achieve?
questions.explain: Fine membrane filters remove yeast and bacteria; coarse depth filters catch larger particles.

questions.q: Which cap management method suits the small open vats often used for Pinot Noir?
questions.explain: Punching down by hand or machine is easy in small open vats.

questions.q: Which flavours are typical of American oak?
questions.explain: American oak, Quercus alba, gives stronger vanilla and coconut than French oak.

questions.q: What can unripe stems add in whole-bunch fermentation?
questions.explain: Ripe stems can add freshness and spice, but unripe ones add green, harsh tannin.

questions.q: In semi-carbonic maceration in Beaujolais, what happens to the lower bunches in the vat?
options: They are crushed by the weight above and ferment normally
They are removed and pressed at once
questions.explain: The lower bunches break and ferment with yeast, while the upper ones undergo carbonic maceration.

questions.q: What happens if the cap is not kept wet during red fermentation?
options: It dries out and can spoil, and extraction stops
It sinks and blocks the press
questions.explain: A dry cap can spoil and no longer gives colour and tannin to the juice.

cards.b: The colour pigments of black grapes, found in the skins.
Holding crushed grapes cool for some days before fermentation to extract colour and fruit. Common for Pinot Noir.
About 20 to 32°C, warmer than white, to help extract colour and tannin.
The layer of skins pushed to the top of the tank by carbon dioxide during red fermentation.
Pumping over: juice from the bottom of the tank is sprayed over the cap.
Punching down: the cap is pushed into the juice by hand or machine.
Rack and return: the juice is drained off and poured back over the cap, which also cools and aerates it.
Softens harsh tannin in red wine. In the EU, egg and milk fining agents must be labelled if detectable.
Fermenting with stems and whole berries. Adds fresh, spicy, herbal notes; unripe stems add green tannin.
Whole bunches under carbon dioxide ferment inside the berry to about 2% alcohol, with cherry and banana aromas.
Whole bunches in a vat: the lower ones are crushed and ferment normally, the upper ones carbonically.
The third Thursday of November of the harvest year.
Leaving the new wine on its skins after fermentation. It extracts more and can make tannins feel softer.
Wine squeezed from the skins after the free-run wine is drained. Darker and more tannic; blended back to taste.
The Bordeaux barrique holds 225 litres; the Bourgogne pièce 228 litres.
Large Italian casks, often of Slavonian oak, traditional for Barolo and Brunello. They add little oak flavour.
French (Quercus petraea, Q. robur) is subtle and spicy. American (Q. alba) gives more vanilla and coconut.

cards.f: Which oak is traditional in Rioja?
cards.b: American oak was long the classic barrel wood of traditional Rioja.
A clay used to fine white wines, removing proteins that could make them hazy.
Notes from bottle ageing, such as leather, earth, forest floor, mushroom and dried fruit.

paths.title: Sparkling, sweet and fortified
paths.summary: How sparkling, sweet and fortified wines are made and labelled: the traditional and tank methods and the EU sweetness terms, noble rot, dried grapes and ice wine, and the ageing categories of Port, Madeira, Sherry and the vins doux naturels.

lessons.title: The traditional method
lessons.intro: This lesson follows a bottle of traditional method sparkling wine from the base wine to the dosage, sets out the EU sweetness terms from Brut Nature to Doux, and compares Champagne with Crémant, Cava and Franciacorta.

p: Good sparkling wine starts with grapes picked early, with high acidity, moderate sugar and delicate flavour. They are pressed gently, usually as whole bunches, so that black grapes give almost clear juice. In Champagne, 4,000 kg of grapes may give at most 2,550 litres of juice: the first 2,050 litres, the cuvée, and then 500 litres of taille.

The juice is fermented into a dry, high-acid still wine of modest alcohol. Then comes blending, or assemblage. Houses blend grapes, villages and often years, and keep reserve wines from earlier harvests so that their non-vintage wine tastes the same from year to year.

At tirage the blend is bottled with the liqueur de tirage, a mix of wine, sugar, yeast and a riddling aid. In Champagne about 24 g/L of sugar is added, enough to build a pressure of around 6 bar. The bottle is sealed, usually with a crown cap.

The second fermentation, the prise de mousse, takes a few weeks in a cool cellar. It adds a little alcohol and traps the carbon dioxide in the wine. The wine is then sold in the bottle in which this fermentation took place, which is what sets the traditional method apart.

After the second fermentation the dead yeast cells, the lees, rest in the bottle. Slowly they break down, a process called autolysis. It gives flavours of bread, brioche, biscuit and toast, a creamier texture and finer bubbles. The longer the ageing, the stronger this character.

Under EU rules, the term traditional method may be used only if the wine stayed on its lees for at least nine months without interruption and was separated from them by disgorgement. Champagne asks for more: non-vintage wine must age at least 15 months after tirage, 12 of them on the lees, and vintage wine at least three years.

Riddling, or remuage, gathers the lees in the neck. On wooden pupitres, bottles are turned and tilted a little at a time until they stand neck down. Today most bottles are riddled in gyropalettes, machines that move hundreds of bottles at once, day and night.

At disgorgement the neck is frozen, the cap is removed and the pressure pushes out the plug of frozen lees. The bottle is topped up with the liqueur d'expédition, wine with or without sugar. This dosage sets the final sweetness, and the bottle is closed with a cork and a wire cage, the muselet.

EU rules define the sweetness terms for sparkling wine by sugar content: Brut Nature under 3 g/L, with no sugar added after the second fermentation; Extra Brut 0 to 6 g/L; Brut under 12 g/L; Extra Dry 12 to 17 g/L; Sec 17 to 32 g/L; Demi-Sec 32 to 50 g/L; and Doux over 50 g/L. Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, despite its name.

Champagne is the model. Its grapes are mainly Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, picked by hand. Styles include non-vintage, vintage, Blanc de Blancs from white grapes, Blanc de Noirs from black grapes, and rosé. Only quarter bottles and very large bottles may be filled from other bottles; every other Champagne is sold in the bottle in which it fermented.

Crémant is a term for traditional method wines made to stricter rules than ordinary sparkling wine: hand-harvested grapes, pressed whole or destemmed at no more than 100 litres of juice per 150 kg, at least nine months on the lees, and under 50 g/L of sugar. France has eight Crémant appellations: Alsace, Bordeaux, Bourgogne, Die, Jura, Limoux, Loire and Savoie. Luxembourg and Belgium, with Crémant de Wallonie, use the term too.

Cava is Spain's traditional method wine. Most comes from Catalonia, around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia in Penedès, but the DO has four zones: Comtats de Barcelona, Valle del Ebro, Viñedos de Almendralejo and Levante. The main grapes are Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Garnacha, Monastrell and Trepat are also allowed.

Cava de Guarda needs at least 9 months on the lees. The top tier, Cava de Guarda Superior, covers Reserva (at least 18 months), Gran Reserva (at least 30 months) and Cava de Paraje Calificado from single sites (at least 36 months). Guarda Superior wines must show the vintage and, from 2025, come from organic vineyards. Gran Reserva and Paraje Calificado may only be Brut Nature, Extra Brut or Brut.

Franciacorta, in Lombardy south of Lake Iseo, is Italy's leading traditional method DOCG. It is made from Chardonnay and Pinot Nero, with up to 50% Pinot Bianco and up to 10% of the local Erbamat. Non-vintage Franciacorta needs at least 18 months on the lees, Satèn and Rosé 24 months, Millesimato 30 and Riserva 60. Satèn is a white from Chardonnay and up to 50% Pinot Bianco, at under 5 atmospheres of pressure and always Brut. Trento DOC and Alta Langa DOCG are other Italian traditional method wines.

key: Champagne press: 4,000 kg of grapes give 2,050 litres of cuvée and 500 litres of taille.
Tirage adds about 24 g/L of sugar for around 6 bar. Autolysis gives bread, brioche and biscuit.
EU traditional method: at least 9 months on the lees. Champagne NV: 15 months after tirage, 12 on the lees; vintage: 3 years.
EU sweetness: Brut Nature under 3, Extra Brut 0 to 6, Brut under 12, Extra Dry 12 to 17, Sec 17 to 32, Demi-Sec 32 to 50, Doux over 50 g/L.
Cava: Guarda 9 months; Guarda Superior is Reserva 18, Gran Reserva 30, Paraje Calificado at least 36 months.
Franciacorta: NV 18 months, Satèn and Rosé 24, Millesimato 30, Riserva 60.

questions.q: What is the sugar limit for Brut under EU rules?
questions.explain: Brut means under 12 g/L. Under 3 g/L is Brut Nature and 12 to 17 g/L is Extra Dry.

questions.q: Which of these terms describes the sweetest sparkling wine?
questions.explain: Extra Dry (12 to 17 g/L) is sweeter than Brut, Extra Brut and Brut Nature.

questions.q: How long must a wine stay on its lees to be called traditional method in the EU?
questions.explain: The EU minimum is nine months on the lees without interruption, with separation by disgorgement.

questions.q: What is the minimum ageing for vintage Champagne?
questions.explain: Vintage Champagne needs at least three years after tirage; non-vintage at least 15 months.

questions.q: How many litres of cuvée may a 4,000 kg press load give in Champagne?
questions.explain: The cuvée is the first 2,050 litres; the taille adds 500 more, for 2,550 in all.

questions.q: What is the minimum lees ageing for Cava Gran Reserva?
questions.explain: Gran Reserva needs 30 months. Reserva needs 18 and Cava de Guarda 9.

questions.q: Which local grape may make up to 10% of Franciacorta?
questions.explain: Erbamat is a late-ripening local variety allowed up to 10%.

questions.q: Which is NOT a condition for the term Crémant?
options: At least nine months on the lees
No more than 100 litres of juice per 150 kg of grapes
Second fermentation in a pressure tank
questions.explain: Crémant must be made by the traditional method, with the second fermentation in bottle.

questions.q: What does a gyropalette do?
options: Riddles hundreds of bottles at once
questions.explain: Gyropalettes do the work of hand riddling on pupitres, day and night.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the eight French Crémant appellations?
questions.explain: The eight are Alsace, Bordeaux, Bourgogne, Die, Jura, Limoux, Loire and Savoie. Champagne has its own appellation.

questions.q: What is the taille in Champagne pressing?
options: The last 500 litres of juice, fruitier and less fine
The yeast sediment in the neck
questions.explain: From 4,000 kg of grapes the cuvée gives 2,050 litres and the taille the last 500.

questions.q: What is the pressure limit for Franciacorta Satèn?
questions.explain: Satèn may not exceed 5 atmospheres, which gives a softer mousse.

questions.q: What is the sugar range of Sec on a sparkling wine label?
questions.explain: Sec is 17 to 32 g/L. Under 12 is Brut, 12 to 17 Extra Dry and 32 to 50 Demi-Sec.

questions.q: Which three grapes make almost all Champagne?
questions.explain: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier dominate; the minor grapes are rare.

questions.q: How is the bottle usually sealed during the second fermentation?
options: With a cork and wire cage
questions.explain: A crown cap is used during tirage; the cork and muselet go on after disgorgement.

questions.q: Which Cava zone produces the great majority of Cava?
questions.explain: Comtats de Barcelona, which includes the heart of Penedès, makes most Cava.

cards.b: The still, dry, high-acid base wine of Champagne before the second fermentation.
4,000 kg of grapes give up to 2,550 litres: 2,050 of cuvée, the finest, and 500 of taille.
NV 18 months, Satèn and Rosé 24, Millesimato 30 and Riserva 60.
Blending base wines from different grapes, villages and years before tirage.
Wines kept from earlier harvests and blended into non-vintage Champagne for a consistent house style.
Wine, sugar, yeast and a riddling aid added at bottling to start the second fermentation.
The second fermentation in the bottle. In Champagne about 24 g/L of sugar gives around 6 bar.
The breakdown of dead yeast cells on the lees, giving bread, brioche and biscuit notes.
Riddling: turning and tilting bottles until the lees collect in the neck, by hand on pupitres or in gyropalettes.
Disgorgement: the neck is frozen and the plug of lees is pushed out when the cap is removed.
Wine, with or without sugar, added after disgorgement. It sets the dosage and final sweetness.
Under 3 g/L of sugar, with no sugar added after the second fermentation. Also dosage zéro or pas dosé.

cards.f: Extra Dry on a sparkling wine
cards.b: 12 to 17 g/L of sugar, so sweeter than Brut despite the name.
Demi-Sec has 32 to 50 g/L of sugar. Doux has more than 50 g/L.
At least 15 months after tirage, 12 of them on the lees.
Hand-picked grapes, at most 100 L of juice per 150 kg, at least 9 months on the lees, under 50 g/L sugar.
Alsace, Bordeaux, Bourgogne, Die, Jura, Limoux, Loire and Savoie.
Mainly Macabeo, Xarel·lo and Parellada; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Garnacha, Monastrell and Trepat also allowed.
Reserva (18 months), Gran Reserva (30) and Paraje Calificado (at least 36): vintage dated and organic.
Chardonnay with up to 50% Pinot Bianco, under 5 atmospheres of pressure and always Brut.

lessons.title: Tank method and other methods
lessons.intro: This lesson covers sparkling wines made without long bottle ageing on the lees: the tank method of Prosecco and Asti, the transfer method, the ancestral method and simple carbonation. It sets out the rules of Prosecco DOC, Prosecco Rosé and the two Prosecco DOCGs.

p: In the tank method, also called the Charmat or Martinotti method, the second fermentation happens in a sealed pressure tank, an autoclave. Base wine, sugar and yeast go into the tank and the carbon dioxide is trapped. The wine is then chilled, filtered and bottled under pressure. Federico Martinotti developed the method in Italy in 1895, and Eugène Charmat improved it in France some years later.

The process is quick and cheap, and the wine spends little or no time on its lees, so it keeps the fresh fruit and floral aromas of the grape. That suits aromatic or delicate varieties. Longer time on the lees in tank, with stirring, can add some texture.
EU law sets pressure bands. Sparkling wine needs at least 3 bar and quality sparkling wine at least 3.5 bar. Semi-sparkling wine, such as frizzante, pétillant or Perlwein, has 1 to 2.5 bar.

Prosecco DOC, created in 2009, covers nine provinces: Treviso, Venezia, Vicenza, Padova and Belluno in the Veneto, and Trieste, Gorizia, Udine and Pordenone in Friuli Venezia Giulia. Glera must make up at least 85%. Up to 15% may come from Verdiso, Bianchetta Trevigiana, Perera, Glera Lunga, Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco, Pinot Grigio and Pinot Nero vinified white. The grape itself was once called Prosecco; the 2009 rules named it Glera so that the place name could be protected.

The styles are Spumante (fully sparkling), Frizzante (semi-sparkling) and still Prosecco. The maximum yield is 18 tonnes per hectare. Spumante may be Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut, Extra Dry, Dry or Demi-Sec. Wine from grapes grown entirely in the province of Treviso or of Trieste, and made and bottled locally, may add that name to the label. Frizzante may also be refermented in the bottle, rifermentazione in bottiglia.

Prosecco Rosé DOC was approved in 2020. It must be Spumante, from 85 to 90% Glera and 10 to 15% Pinot Nero vinified as red. The second fermentation must last at least 60 days in tank. The wine must be labelled Millesimato with its vintage, at least 85% from the stated year, and may be Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut or Extra Dry. It may be sold from 1 January after the harvest.

Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG covers the steep hills of 15 communes between the two towns, in the province of Treviso. The landscape, Le Colline del Prosecco di Conegliano e Valdobbiadene, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019. Rive marks wine from one commune or one of its hamlets, and there are 43 Rive. Superiore di Cartizze comes from about 107 hectares of the steepest slopes of Valdobbiadene.

Most DOCG wine is Spumante, made Extra Brut, Brut, Extra Dry or Dry. Frizzante and still wines are also made. Sui Lieviti is refermented in the bottle and keeps its yeast sediment, the old col fondo style, and is Brut Nature.

Asolo Prosecco DOCG, also called Colli Asolani, lies on the hills around Asolo in 18 communes of the province of Treviso, west of the Piave. It was the first Prosecco denomination to allow the Extra Brut style.

Asti DOCG, in Piemonte, is made from Moscato Bianco. Here the pressure tank is used in a different way, with a single fermentation. Grape must ferments in the sealed tank, the carbon dioxide is trapped, and fermentation is stopped by chilling and filtering while much grape sugar remains.

Classic Asti is fully sparkling and sweet, with about 7 to 9.5% alcohol. Moscato d'Asti is only lightly sparkling, usually sweeter and lower in alcohol, at around 5%. Both smell of grapes, peach and orange blossom and are best drunk young. Drier versions are allowed too: Asti Secco was approved in 2017.

In the transfer method, the second fermentation takes place in bottle as in the traditional method. The bottles are then emptied into a pressure tank, the wine is filtered off its lees and filled into new bottles. It avoids riddling and disgorgement and evens out differences between bottles. Under EU rules such wine may be called bottle-fermented, but not traditional method, because the lees are removed by filtering rather than disgorgement.

The ancestral method is older than Champagne's. There is only one fermentation: it starts in tank, the wine is bottled before it is finished, and the fermentation ends in the bottle, trapping the carbon dioxide. Clairette de Die méthode ancestrale, made mainly from Muscat à Petits Grains, is slowed by cold, ages at least four months on its lees in bottle and keeps sweetness at about 7 to 9% alcohol. Blanquette de Limoux méthode ancestrale is made from Mauzac, and Gaillac also has a méthode ancestrale. Pétillant naturel, or pét-nat, is a modern name for the style.

The cheapest sparkling wines are carbonated: carbon dioxide is injected into still wine. The bubbles are larger and fade quickly, and EU labels must say the wine was obtained by adding carbon dioxide.

key: Tank (Charmat or Martinotti) method: second fermentation in a pressure tank; fresh fruit and little autolysis.
EU pressure: sparkling at least 3 bar, quality sparkling at least 3.5 bar, semi-sparkling 1 to 2.5 bar.
Prosecco DOC (2009): nine provinces in the Veneto and Friuli Venezia Giulia, at least 85% Glera, up to 18 t/ha.
Prosecco Rosé DOC (2020): Spumante, 10 to 15% Pinot Nero, at least 60 days in tank, always Millesimato, Brut Nature to Extra Dry.
Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG: 15 communes, 43 Rive, Cartizze about 107 ha, UNESCO 2019. Asolo DOCG was first with Extra Brut.
Asti: one fermentation stopped by chilling. Transfer: bottle-fermented, filtered in tank. Ancestral: one fermentation finished in bottle.

questions.q: What share of Pinot Nero must Prosecco Rosé DOC contain?
questions.explain: Prosecco Rosé is 85 to 90% Glera with 10 to 15% Pinot Nero vinified as red.

questions.q: How long must the second fermentation of Prosecco Rosé last in tank?
questions.explain: The rules ask for at least 60 days in tank for the rosé.

questions.q: Which of these provinces is NOT part of Prosecco DOC?
questions.explain: The nine provinces are Treviso, Venezia, Vicenza, Padova, Belluno, Trieste, Gorizia, Udine and Pordenone.

questions.q: What does Rive mean on a Conegliano Valdobbiadene label?
options: A wine aged three years on its lees
Wine from one commune or one of its hamlets
questions.explain: There are 43 Rive, each a commune or hamlet within the DOCG.

questions.q: How does Asti differ from most Prosecco in the way it is made?
options: It has a single fermentation of grape must, stopped by chilling
It is made from dried grapes
questions.explain: Asti ferments the must only once in a sealed tank and is stopped while sweet.

questions.q: Which grape is Blanquette de Limoux méthode ancestrale made from?
questions.explain: Mauzac is the grape of Blanquette de Limoux. Muscat à Petits Grains leads in Clairette de Die.

questions.q: What is the minimum pressure for EU quality sparkling wine?
questions.explain: Quality sparkling wine needs at least 3.5 bar; ordinary sparkling wine 3 bar; semi-sparkling 1 to 2.5 bar.

questions.q: Why may transfer method wine not be called traditional method in the EU?
options: The second fermentation happens in tank
The lees are removed by filtering in tank, not by disgorgement
questions.explain: The traditional method term requires disgorgement. Transfer method wine may be called bottle-fermented.

questions.q: Which Prosecco landscape became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019?
options: The hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene
questions.explain: Le Colline del Prosecco di Conegliano e Valdobbiadene were listed in 2019.

questions.q: In which year was Prosecco DOC created?
questions.explain: Prosecco DOC and the two DOCGs date from 2009. 2020 is the year Prosecco Rosé was approved.

questions.q: About how much alcohol does Asti have?
questions.explain: Asti has about 7 to 9.5% alcohol. Moscato d'Asti is lower, at around 5%.

questions.q: Which sweetness level is NOT allowed for Prosecco Rosé DOC?
questions.explain: Prosecco Rosé may be Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut or Extra Dry. White Spumante may also be Dry or Demi-Sec.

questions.q: Why does tank method wine keep fresh fruit aromas?
options: It spends little or no time on its lees
It is made from dried grapes
questions.explain: With little lees contact there is little autolysis, so primary fruit leads.

questions.q: How long must Clairette de Die méthode ancestrale stay on its lees in bottle?
questions.explain: The rules ask for at least four months on the lees in bottle before release.

questions.q: What does rifermentazione in bottiglia mean on a Prosecco Frizzante label?
options: The wine was refermented in the bottle
questions.explain: The second fermentation took place in the bottle, not in a tank, so the wine may be slightly hazy.

questions.q: Which was the first Prosecco denomination to allow the Extra Brut style?
questions.explain: Asolo Prosecco DOCG, also called Colli Asolani, led the way with Extra Brut.

cards.b: Second fermentation in a sealed pressure tank, then filtering and bottling under pressure. Also Charmat or Martinotti.
The sealed pressure tank used for the tank method.
Italian who developed the tank method in 1895. Eugène Charmat improved it in France some years later.
Sparkling at least 3 bar, quality sparkling at least 3.5 bar, semi-sparkling 1 to 2.5 bar.
The main grape of Prosecco, at least 85%. It was called Prosecco until the 2009 rules renamed it.
Nine provinces, five in the Veneto and four in Friuli Venezia Giulia. Created in 2009.
18 tonnes of grapes per hectare.
Allowed when all the grapes come from that province and the wine is made and bottled locally.
Approved in 2020: Spumante only, 85 to 90% Glera and 10 to 15% Pinot Nero vinified as red.
At least 60 days in tank, always labelled Millesimato, sold from 1 January after harvest.
Brut Nature, Extra Brut, Brut or Extra Dry. White Prosecco Spumante may also be Dry or Demi-Sec.
Vintage-dated Prosecco, with at least 85% of the wine from the stated year.
Steep hills in 15 communes of Treviso. Its landscape became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.
Prosecco Superiore from one commune or hamlet. There are 43 Rive.
About 107 ha on the steepest hills of Valdobbiadene, the most prized Prosecco site.
Prosecco Superiore refermented in bottle and left on its yeast sediment, Brut Nature. The old col fondo style.
Hills around Asolo in Treviso, also called Colli Asolani. The first Prosecco to allow Extra Brut.
Sweet, lightly sparkling Moscato Bianco from Piemonte, at about 5% alcohol.
One fermentation that starts in tank and finishes in bottle. Clairette de Die and Limoux are classic examples.
Bottle fermentation, then the wine is emptied into a tank, filtered and rebottled. Bottle-fermented, not traditional.

lessons.title: Sweet wines
lessons.intro: This lesson covers the ways to make a sweet wine: late harvest, noble rot, dried grapes and frozen grapes, with the rules of Sauternes, Tokaj, the German Prädikate and ice wine. It ends with how winemakers keep the sweetness, by stopping fermentation or by adding spirit.

p: A wine is sweet when sugar is left after fermentation. Either the grapes are so rich in sugar that the yeast cannot ferment it all, or the winemaker stops fermentation early. The greatest sweet wines combine high sugar with high acidity, which keeps them fresh rather than cloying.

Sugar is concentrated in four main ways: by leaving grapes to ripen and shrivel on the vine, by noble rot, by drying the grapes after harvest, and by freezing them on the vine. Each gives its own flavours.

Grapes left on the vine after the normal harvest keep gaining sugar and lose water. Late in autumn the berries may shrivel on the vine, a process called passerillage. In Germany, Spätlese means late harvest, though today the term is set by must weight rather than a picking date.

Alsace Vendanges Tardives and the richer Sélection de Grains Nobles come from very ripe Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris or Muscat. In Jurançon, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, Petit Manseng and Gros Manseng are left to shrivel on the vine for sweet wines with vivid acidity.

Noble rot is Botrytis cinerea on ripe, healthy grapes in the right weather: misty, humid mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons. The fungus pierces the skins and water evaporates, so sugar, acidity and glycerol become concentrated. It adds flavours of honey, marmalade, saffron and dried apricot. Infection is uneven, so pickers make several passes.

Sauternes, with Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac, lies where the cool Ciron meets the warmer Garonne. The grapes are Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle, picked by hand in successive tries. The must needs at least 221 g/L of sugar, the wine at least 12% alcohol and 45 g/L of sugar, and the maximum yield is only 25 hl/ha. Barsac may be sold under its own name or as Sauternes.

Tokaji Aszú, from Tokaj in north-east Hungary, is made mainly from Furmint and Hárslevelű. Nobly rotten aszú berries are picked one by one and soaked in fermenting must or wine. Since the 2013 harvest Aszú must have at least 120 g/L of sugar, the old 5 puttonyos level, and spend at least 18 months in cask, so only 5 and 6 puttonyos remain on labels. Eszencia, the syrup that runs from aszú berries under their own weight, has at least 450 g/L of sugar and very little alcohol.

In Germany, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese come from individually picked, usually botrytised berries. TBA needs a must weight of about 150 to 154 °Oechsle, depending on region and grape. Austria's Neusiedlersee and the Coteaux du Layon in the Loire, with Quarts de Chaume and Bonnezeaux, are other noble rot regions.

Grapes can be dried after picking, in airy lofts, on racks, on straw mats or in the sun. They lose water and concentrate sugar, acid and flavour, and gain notes of raisin, fig and nuts. In Italy this is called appassimento.

Recioto della Valpolicella is a sweet red from dried Corvina and its partners, the older sibling of the dry Amarone. Recioto di Soave is a sweet white from dried Garganega. Vin Santo, in Toscana, is made from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia and aged for years in small sealed barrels called caratelli, often with deliberate oxidation. A rosé version from Sangiovese is called Occhio di Pernice.

Passito di Pantelleria comes from Zibibbo, the local name of Muscat of Alexandria, grown on a windy volcanic island between Sicily and Tunisia; some of the grapes are dried in the sun. The Jura makes vin de paille, and Austria Strohwein and Schilfwein, from grapes dried on straw or reeds.

For ice wine the grapes stay on the vine into winter and are picked and pressed while frozen. Most of the water stays behind as ice, so only a little very sweet, high-acid juice runs from the press. The grapes must be healthy, and classic ice wine has little or no noble rot.

German Eiswein must reach the same minimum must weight as Beerenauslese, from grapes frozen when picked and pressed. In Canada, VQA Icewine, mostly from the Niagara Peninsula in Ontario and often from Vidal or Riesling, needs grapes naturally frozen on the vine and picked at -8°C or colder. Freezing grapes artificially is not allowed for either name.

Sometimes fermentation stops by itself: in very sweet musts the yeast struggles as alcohol rises, and Sauternes usually stops at around 13 to 14% alcohol. More often the winemaker stops it by chilling the wine, adding sulphur dioxide and filtering out the yeast. Many fruity Mosel Rieslings and Moscato d'Asti are made this way.

In Germany some wines are sweetened with Süssreserve, unfermented grape juice added before bottling. The other route is fortification. Adding grape spirit during fermentation stops the yeast and keeps natural grape sugar, as in Port and the vins doux naturels of France.

key: Sugar is concentrated by late harvest, noble rot, drying or freezing, and kept by stopping fermentation or by fortifying.
Noble rot needs misty mornings and dry afternoons. Sauternes: at least 221 g/L sugar in the must, at most 25 hl/ha, hand-picked tries.
Tokaji Aszú since 2013: at least 120 g/L sugar and 18 months in cask. Eszencia: at least 450 g/L.
TBA needs about 150 to 154 °Oechsle; Eiswein matches the Beerenauslese minimum.
Dried grapes: Recioto, Vin Santo (caratelli), Passito di Pantelleria (Zibibbo), vin de paille, Strohwein.
Canadian VQA Icewine: grapes naturally frozen and picked at -8°C or colder. No artificial freezing.

questions.q: What minimum sugar must Tokaji Aszú have since the 2013 harvest?
questions.explain: Since 2013 every Aszú needs at least 120 g/L, the old 5 puttonyos level. 450 g/L is the Eszencia minimum.

questions.q: What is the maximum yield for Sauternes?
questions.explain: Sauternes allows just 25 hl/ha, which reflects how little juice nobly rotten grapes give.

questions.q: Which grape makes Passito di Pantelleria?
questions.explain: Zibibbo is the local name of Muscat of Alexandria on Pantelleria.

questions.q: At what temperature must grapes for Canadian VQA Icewine be picked?
questions.explain: VQA rules require grapes naturally frozen on the vine and picked at -8°C or colder.

questions.q: What are caratelli?
options: Small sealed barrels used to age Vin Santo
Straw mats used in the Jura
questions.explain: Vin Santo ages for years in small caratelli, often with deliberate oxidation.

questions.q: Which grape is left to shrivel on the vine for sweet Jurançon?
questions.explain: Petit Manseng, with Gros Manseng, shrivels on the vine in Jurançon and keeps high acidity.

questions.q: Which German Prädikat needs a must weight of about 150 to 154 °Oechsle?
questions.explain: TBA has the highest must weight. Eiswein shares the Beerenauslese minimum.

questions.q: What is Süssreserve?
options: A noble rot wine from Austria
Unfermented grape juice added to sweeten a wine
The syrup that runs from aszú berries
questions.explain: Süssreserve is sterile, unfermented grape juice blended in before bottling.

questions.q: At about what alcohol does the fermentation of Sauternes usually stop?
questions.explain: In very sweet musts the yeast struggles as alcohol rises, and Sauternes usually stops at around 13 to 14%.

questions.q: From which harvest did Tokaji Aszú lose its 3 and 4 puttonyos levels?
questions.explain: From the 2013 harvest Aszú needs at least 120 g/L of sugar, so only 5 and 6 puttonyos remain.

questions.q: Which Alsace term means late harvest?
questions.explain: Vendanges Tardives is late harvest; Sélection de Grains Nobles is the richer, usually botrytised level.

questions.q: What is the minimum sugar in the must for Sauternes?
questions.explain: Sauternes musts need at least 221 g/L of sugar. 120 g/L is the Tokaji Aszú minimum and 450 g/L the Eszencia minimum.

questions.q: What is Recioto di Soave made from?
questions.explain: Recioto di Soave is a sweet white DOCG from dried Garganega. Dried Corvina makes Recioto della Valpolicella.

questions.q: What keeps great sweet wines fresh rather than cloying?
questions.explain: High acidity balances the sugar, as in Sauternes, Tokaji and German Riesling.

questions.q: What is Occhio di Pernice?
options: A rosé Vin Santo from Sangiovese
questions.explain: Occhio di Pernice is the rosé version of Vin Santo, made mainly from Sangiovese.

questions.q: Which Prädikat's minimum must weight must German Eiswein reach?
questions.explain: Eiswein shares the Beerenauslese minimum must weight.

cards.b: Shrivelling of grapes on the vine, which concentrates sugar. Used in Jurançon and for late harvest wines.
Alsace late harvest wine from Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris or Muscat.
The richer Alsace sweet wine, usually from nobly rotten grapes of the four noble varieties.
Pyrenean foothill appellation whose sweet wines come from Petit and Gros Manseng shrivelled on the vine.
The fungus behind grey rot in wet weather and noble rot when misty mornings give way to dry afternoons.
Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Sauvignon Gris and Muscadelle.
At least 221 g/L of sugar in the must and a maximum yield of 25 hl/ha.
Sauternes, Barsac, Bommes, Fargues and Preignac. Barsac may also use its own name.
Mainly Furmint and Hárslevelű, with Sárgamuskotály (Yellow Muscat), Zéta, Kövérszőlő and Kabar.
A hod of aszú berries. Since 2013 Aszú needs 120 g/L of sugar, so only 5 and 6 puttonyos remain.
Syrup that runs from aszú berries, with at least 450 g/L of sugar. It ferments very slowly to low alcohol.
Shrivelled, botrytised berries picked one by one. Must weight about 150 to 154 °Oechsle.
Overripe, usually botrytised berries picked one by one. Must weight about 110 to 128 °Oechsle.
Grapes frozen on the vine and pressed while frozen. Same minimum must weight as Beerenauslese.
VQA rules: grapes naturally frozen and picked at -8°C or colder, often Vidal or Riesling.
Drying grapes after harvest to concentrate sugar and flavour, used for Recioto and Amarone.
Sweet red DOCG from dried Corvina and its partners. Amarone is the dry version.
Sweet white DOCG from dried Garganega grapes.
Toscana's sweet wine from dried Trebbiano and Malvasia, aged in caratelli. Occhio di Pernice is the rosé.
Sweet Zibibbo (Muscat of Alexandria) from a volcanic island between Sicily and Tunisia.

lessons.title: Port and Madeira
lessons.intro: This lesson covers how Port is made, its two families of style, ruby and tawny, and the official ageing categories. It then turns to Madeira: its grapes, its heating by estufagem or canteiro, and its age statements.

p: Port comes from the Douro valley in northern Portugal, demarcated in 1756 under the Marquês de Pombal. Vines grow on terraces of schist in a hot, dry summer climate. Porto is the PDO for the fortified wine and Douro the PDO for the region's unfortified wines. Both are regulated by the Instituto dos Vinhos do Douro e do Porto (IVDP).

Many grapes are allowed. The leading black grapes are Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca and Tinto Cão. White Port uses grapes such as Malvasia Fina, Gouveio, Viosinho and Rabigato.

Fermentation lasts only two or three days, so colour and tannin must be extracted fast. Grapes are trodden by foot in shallow granite troughs called lagares, worked by robotic pistons in mechanical lagares, or pumped over in tanks. When the right amount of sugar remains, the wine is run onto grape spirit, aguardente, of about 77% abv, at roughly one part spirit to four parts wine.

The spirit stops the fermentation and leaves a sweet wine of 19 to 22% abv. The young Port is then aged in the Douro or, traditionally, in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, across the river from the city of Porto.

Ruby Ports age in large vats or tanks, with little contact with oxygen, and keep deep colour and black fruit. Basic Ruby is young and blended. Reserve Ruby is a higher quality blend approved by the IVDP tasting panel.

Late Bottled Vintage (LBV) comes from a single year and is bottled between the fourth and sixth year after the harvest. Most LBV is filtered and ready to drink. Unfiltered LBV can improve in bottle and, after at least three years in bottle, may be labelled bottle matured.

Vintage Port comes from a single year of top quality, declared by the shipper and approved by the IVDP. It is bottled in its second or third year, unfiltered, and matures for decades in bottle, throwing a heavy deposit that needs decanting. Single Quinta Vintage Port comes from one estate, often in years that are not generally declared. Crusted Port is a blend of several years, bottled unfiltered and kept at least three years in bottle before sale.
Tawny Ports age in casks called pipes, where slow oxidation turns them amber and gives flavours of nuts, toffee, dried fruit and spice. They are ready to drink when bottled and do not need decanting.

Reserve Tawny has spent at least seven years in wood. Tawny with an indication of age may be labelled 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years old, and since 2022 a Very Very Old category exists for wines of at least 80 years. The age is not an exact average: it describes the character of the blend, which the IVDP tasting panel must approve.

Colheita is a tawny from a single harvest, aged at least seven years in wood, with both the harvest year and the year of bottling on the label. White Port can be dry or sweet and also exists with age indications and as Colheita. Rosé Port is a young style made with brief skin contact.

sections.h: Madeira: the island and its grapes
p: Madeira is a Portuguese island in the Atlantic, west of Morocco. Its wine became famous in the 18th century, when shippers found that casks carried through the tropics came back improved by the heat and the motion. Today the heating is done on the island.

Four noble white grapes name four styles of sweetness. Sercial is the driest, then Verdelho (medium dry), Boal or Bual (medium sweet) and Malvasia or Malmsey (sweet). Terrantez is a rare fifth. Tinta Negra, a black grape, makes most of the wine.

Fermentation is stopped with neutral grape spirit of 96% abv. Sweet styles are fortified early, after about a day, and drier styles ferment for longer first. High natural acidity keeps even the sweetest Madeira fresh.

In estufagem the wine is heated in tanks, usually to 45 to 50°C and never above 50°C, for at least three months, then left to rest. It is the quicker method, used for most younger wines. In canteiro the wine ages in casks in warm lofts, heated only by the sun, for years and often for decades. The finest Madeira is made this way.

Blends carry age statements of 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40 and over 50 years. Colheita, or Harvest, comes from a single year and ages at least five years. Frasqueira, also called Garrafeira, is vintage Madeira aged at least 20 years in cask. Because Madeira is already heated and oxidised, it lasts for decades and keeps for a long time after opening.

key: The Douro was demarcated in 1756. Port is fortified during fermentation with spirit of about 77% to 19 to 22% abv.
LBV: one year, bottled in the 4th to 6th year. Vintage: a declared year, bottled in the 2nd or 3rd year.
Crusted: a blend of years, unfiltered, at least 3 years in bottle before sale.
Tawny: Reserve at least 7 years in wood; 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 years; Very Very Old (80+) since 2022. Colheita: one year, at least 7 years in wood.
Madeira from dry to sweet: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia. Tinta Negra makes most of the wine.
Estufagem: 45 to 50°C, never above 50°C, for at least 3 months. Canteiro: casks in warm lofts, for years. Frasqueira: at least 20 years in cask.

questions.q: When must LBV Port be bottled?
options: In the second or third year after harvest
Between the fourth and sixth year after harvest
After at least seven years in wood
questions.explain: LBV comes from one year and is bottled four to six years after harvest. Vintage Port is bottled in its second or third year.

questions.q: About how strong is the grape spirit used to fortify Port?
questions.explain: Port uses aguardente of about 77%. Madeira and the vins doux naturels use neutral spirit of about 96%.

questions.q: Which Port is a blend of several years, bottled unfiltered and aged at least three years in bottle before sale?
questions.explain: Crusted Port blends years, is bottled unfiltered and throws a crust in bottle.

questions.q: What is the minimum time in wood for a Colheita Port?
questions.explain: Colheita is a single-harvest tawny aged at least seven years in wood.

questions.q: Which category did the IVDP add in 2022 for the oldest tawnies?
questions.explain: Since 2022 tawnies of at least 80 years may be labelled Very Very Old, alongside the new 50 years category. VORS is a Sherry term.

questions.q: Which Madeira grape gives the driest style?
questions.explain: Sercial is the driest, then Verdelho, Boal and Malvasia (Malmsey), the sweetest.

questions.q: In estufagem, Madeira is heated to about which temperature for at least three months?
questions.explain: Estufagem heats the wine to about 45 to 50°C, never above 50°C. Canteiro uses only the warmth of the lofts.

questions.q: What is Frasqueira Madeira?
options: A Madeira heated in an estufa
Vintage Madeira aged at least 20 years in cask
An unfortified wine of the island
questions.explain: Frasqueira, or Garrafeira, is vintage Madeira with at least 20 years in cask.

questions.q: What is a lagar?
options: A Port lodge in Vila Nova de Gaia
A shallow granite trough for treading grapes
questions.explain: Treading in lagares extracts colour and tannin quickly during the short fermentation.

questions.q: What is canteiro?
options: Heating the wine in tanks at 45 to 50°C
Ageing in casks in warm lofts, heated only by the sun
Blending several years in a solera
questions.explain: Canteiro is the slow method used for the finest Madeira, often for decades in cask.

questions.q: When may an unfiltered LBV be labelled bottle matured?
options: After at least three years in bottle
questions.explain: Under IVDP rules the term needs at least three years of ageing in bottle.

questions.q: Which Port comes from one estate, often in years that are not generally declared?
questions.explain: Single Quinta Vintage Port comes from one quinta, often in good but undeclared years.

questions.q: What alcohol does Port usually have?
questions.explain: Fortification with spirit of about 77% leaves Port at 19 to 22% abv.

questions.q: Which Madeira style is the sweetest?
questions.explain: Malvasia (Malmsey) is the sweetest, after Sercial, Verdelho and Boal.

questions.q: In which year was the Douro demarcated?
questions.explain: The Douro was demarcated in 1756 under the Marquês de Pombal.

questions.q: How strong is the spirit used to stop fermentation in Madeira?
questions.explain: Madeira uses neutral grape spirit of 96%. Port uses aguardente of about 77%.

Porto is the PDO for the fortified wine; Douro is the PDO for the region's unfortified wines.
Instituto dos Vinhos do Douro e do Porto, which regulates Port and Douro wines and approves the special categories.
